Title: How to Fix Protect Thine Own

Messages.Author: Jeff Kuta
Messages.Body:
Protect Thine Own
Political Action
Cost: 1 blood
Worth 1 vote. Called by any Justicar or Inner Circle member at +1
stealth.
Choose a Non-Camarilla vampire with a capacity below 6. If the acting
vampire is a member of the Inner Circle, you may choose any
Non-Camarilla vampire instead. If this referendum is successful, burn
that vampire.

Let's all assume this card is broken for the sake of discussion. What
changes would be required to "unbreak" it?

How about this (changes in <>):
Protect Thine Own
Political Action
Cost: <X> blood
Worth 1 vote. Called by any Justicar or Inner Circle member at +1
stealth.
Choose a Non-Camarilla vampire with a capacity below <X>. Justicars
may only choose Non-Camarilla vampires with capacity below 6. If this
referendum is successful, burn that vampire.

Messages.Author: John P.
Messages.Body:
"Jeff Kuta" <jeff...@hotmail.com> wrote in message news:621dd332.0312...@posting.google.com...

> Let's all assume this card is broken for the sake of discussion. What
> changes would be required to "unbreak" it?

Rather than address the mechanics of the fix the more useful
option for those seeking to have it fixed would be to figure out
how to get the VEKN/White Wolf to agree to change and or ban
the card. I think once WW decides to change the card they would
be able to come up with the "how" on their own. (good thing/bad thing?)

The philosophy in the past appears to have been that a card is not dealt with
until it's "brokeness" is prevalent in the tournament scene. However with
PTO demonstrating its "brokeness" in the tournament scene is difficult for
one main reason:

Its effectiveness depends on what vampires opponents are playing and given that
PTO seems to becoming more common more people may be playing camarilla
decks to avoid its effects. Thus the "brokeness" of PTO hides in people countering
the card by avoiding vulnerability (playing cammies). But a sign of PTOs brokeness
should then be the diversity that decreases in decks. Tracing this however back to PTO
would be difficult at best.

So we are left with a couple of options (and this is by no means a complete list
and sugestions are encouraged:
1) go through our local princes to have them make requests for change
(could combine with #2 with prince's conducting polls of their players)
2) some type of petition or poll to demonstrate concern or lack thereof to
White Wolf/VEKN (would need some for of prevention for fraud)
3) Continue as is with random beseechings/rants on newsgroups/forums/boards
in the hope that change occurs.

Does anybody have any indication from the appropriate people that WW/VEKN
is concerned about the card? Or are they just amused by our ravings and don't see
the problem. The problem is not in how to fix the problem caused by the card, but
how to attract notice to the problem so that it will be fixed, and I'm not entirely
certain that posts to this newsgroup will get the job done.

And for the record I would like to see the card banned or severely restricted in use.

-JTP

Messages.Author: The Fanboy
Messages.Body:
Protect Thine Own
Political Action

Cost: 1 pool

Worth 1 vote. Called by any Justicar or Inner Circle member at +1
stealth.

Cards may not be played during the referandum. Choose a Non-Camarilla
vampire controlled by your predator or prey with a capacity below 6.

If the acting vampire is a member of the Inner Circle, you may choose
any

Non-Camarilla vampire controlled by your predator or prey instead. If
this referendum is successful, burn that vampire, and its controller
gains pool equal to half the capacity of that vampire (rounded down).

1) This eliminates cross-table "because I can" unbalancing.
2) It reduces the drastic impact it has on the table -- instead of
being potentially an 11-pool slam (making it as unbalancing as Return
to Innocence), it hits your prey or predator for a variable
pool-equivalent resource drain, putting it on par with other vote
cards.
3) It's harder to pass, as it cannot be pushed through normal means,
and non-Cam vampires can't be shut out of the referendum. But it's
still passable if you have vote lock or negotiate with allies for
their votes.
4) The cost is more relevant.

I would still use the card with this text. It would still have a
considerable effect if used offensively. But it won't ruin my entire
game like the current version does if used against me.

Fanboy

I don't care if my predator or prey gains 5 pool for Lazverinus,
Thetmes, Goratrix, or Cailean. That vampire is off the table and
staying there, and THAT effect is all I'm really after. I can bleed
through the extra 5 pool, I'm Arika.

>1) This eliminates cross-table "because I can" unbalancing.

True -- you now at least force someone to have the stealth or Daring the
Dawn in hand.

>2) It reduces the drastic impact it has on the table -- instead of
>being potentially an 11-pool slam (making it as unbalancing as Return
>to Innocence), it hits your prey or predator for a variable
>pool-equivalent resource drain, putting it on par with other vote
>cards.

There's no vote card that provides this effect. Your minion and all the
kit-ups on him are gone forever, and pool gain just isn't much of an
offset -- the 10-caps this gets used on are lynchpin vampires. 3 turns
later without your key vampire, you're dead.

Compare to Banishment -- it's possible to get the minion back same as it
was before, and you can usually get it back much faster since it was
often half full.

>3) It's harder to pass, as it cannot be pushed through normal means,
>and non-Cam vampires can't be shut out of the referendum. But it's
>still passable if you have vote lock or negotiate with allies for
>their votes.

Sure, you can't force it through with Awe, but vote lock shouldn't be
THAT hard to gain.

>4) The cost is more relevant.

1 pool and 1 blood are equivalent in this context. 3 pool and +5 to my
prey would be worth it to get his Cailean off the table and gone for
good.

>I would still use the card with this text. It would still have a
>considerable effect if used offensively. But it won't ruin my entire
>game like the current version does if used against me.

Why not? So you get 5 pool for your Cailean with 2 Raven Spies and a
Mark V. Big deal -- that's 5 pool slower that you'll be ousted.

A race? Nonono... there is a race to play Giant's Blood. There is a

Ancient Influence before your prey gets out a big cap. But these are
cards that any deck can play.

Not every deck has Justicars and Inner Circle in them. Not every deck
can effectively fit them in.

Cheesiest, yes. But not broken. Not when you still need the pool to
get out an 11-cap, the stealth to get past blockers, the prayers
answered that your prey or predator has a worthy non-Cam target, the
votes to get the vote called, and the prayers to be answered that some
schmuck doesn't have the cheesiest of reaction cards, Delaying
Tactics, in their hand.

Hell, if it's so broken, why didn't I even see one at the last Aussie
Nationals. I have 3 of them, I could have built a deck with them
easily, but I didn't. Because having a PTO deck does NOT guarentee
victory. It does NOT make it sure thang. Not even close. If there
is an average possibility that a PTO deck can lose, then it's not
broken. Dented, comes loose, files down, threads wear down, but not
broken.

ugh, of all the whining done on this group posting, I swear the ones
that hurt my ears the most are the ones complaining about this card
and that card.

Messages.Author: Snapcase
Messages.Body:
In article <bspr05$u$1...@reader08.wxs.nl>, dontfe...@spam.me says...

> Part of the problem is, that the current metagame relies on small and
> midcap vampires, which tend not to have votes.

Depends where your metagame is.

> That's why vote lock is so easy to get. And a IC *and* a Justicar? How
> often do you see someone have both in play and ready?

IC is often a vote lock to begin with. That's 5 votes every time you
play a vote card, and nothing else. And the justicar usually comes out
because the IC member governs down to it.

> How is this different from, say, a 4 cap POT dude rushing your precious
> Cailean, doing the typical Signpost/IG/Pushing the Limit/Disarm thing?

Cailean sets range, laughs at POT dude, hits him with some crows and
bats and continues on his merry way.

> Sure it requires more cards and a combat so you can defend yourself.
> That's because you include combat defense cards in your deck. You DO
> play with defense vs politics right?

What are the options of vote defense?

1. Delaying Tactics. They'll call it next turn, and just bleed you for
a shitload this turn. Or govern out the aforementioned justicar.
2. Vox Domini. May make a decent sized splash, but can only play 1 per
game. Basically it's DI for a single vote.
3. Reactive/out of turn vote gaining cards. These generally suck, and
can be countered by playing action modifier vote gaining cards (which
will probably occur anyway).
4. Blocking. Undoubtedly the best option, although all 4 of the IC
members I see regularly have a stealth discipline. Obfuscate has access
to "your block fails" and protean has access to "combat ends, continue
as if unblocked".
5. Smacking down the vampires taking the political actions. Oops.
Can't do that. Lazverinus got burned.

> Losing your only guy is a inherent weakness of playing with big
> vampires. There should be rewards as well. Is there ANY reason to play
> with an IC member AT ALL if PtO didn't exist?

Let's see. Lots of disciplines. 4 sitting votes. +2 sitting bleed.
Useful special abilities (Leandro/Arika). Looks solid to me...

> If HE loses his Arika to, say, not having an Obedience in hand and getting
> wasted in a rush, that
> deck ends right there. Pentex Subversion? All this can happen to your
> Cailean too. Not a problem, I'd say.

Arika can kill Cailean with a PtO. There is no easily usable equivalent
card to kill Arika that doesn't kill Cailean. Fear of Mekhet is neat.
It also affects a grand total of 21 vampires as opposed to the 699 that
can be burned by PTO. Bit of a disparity in opportunity cost. Hell,
Fear isn't even a sure burn.

> > Sure, you can't force it through with Awe, but vote lock shouldn't be
> > THAT hard to gain.
>
> Again, that's because everyone plays with small midcaps.

If everyone was playing with small to midcaps, nobody would be
complaining about PTO.

> So you block with your Cailean, go to long, fire the Mark V, opponent
> play Mayapayatewyrfhewu and Amaranth. He's gone as well. You won't even
> gain 5 pool.

Elder Impersonation. Oops. Your block fails.

> You go equip that Raven spy, you get blocked by some stinking Tzim, who
> play BotD and Rotschrek. In his turn he eats him with Horatio. No 5 pool
> either.

Or you could play stealth. They do have obfuscate, you know.

> The reason people don't use big vampires is because they are too easy to
> kill. PtO is just another way.

PtO also has the fewest counters, and early on only requires a single
card or a two card combination.

--
-Snapcase

Messages.Author: David Cherryholmes
Messages.Body:
On Mon, 29 Dec 2003, Ulugh Beg II wrote:

> Part of the problem is, that the current metagame relies on small and
> midcap vampires, which tend not to have votes.
> That's why vote lock is so easy to get. And a IC *and* a Justicar? How
> often do you see someone have both in play and ready?

All the time. Locally, it's usually Alexandra and Anneke, and Anson,
too. Please don't ask me to explain how he can afford all those
minions. It's called "Unblockable Voter Cap". The other guy plays Arika
and Democritus about one game out of four. Yes, I know Democritus is ass,
and I've told him so, but it's the answer to your question. In any case,
most vote decks build a solid base of table votes, and *then* push off
that. Often, the push is gratuitous.

> How is this different from, say, a 4 cap POT dude rushing your precious
> Cailean, doing the typical Signpost/IG/Pushing the Limit/Disarm thing?
> Sure it requires more cards and a combat so you can defend yourself.
> That's because you include combat defense cards in your deck. You DO
> play with defense vs politics right?

Well, for one thing, Cailean sets range to long and laughs at them, at the
very least. Cailean is just about impossible to put down with straight
combat. That's why he's a ten cap with no title and no bounce. Oh, but
you're playing PTO. Right.

> Losing your only guy is a inherent weakness of playing with big
> vampires. There should be rewards as well. Is there ANY reason to play
> with an IC member AT ALL if PtO didn't exist?

This can *not* be a serious fucking question. More disciplines than
god? 4 votes? 3 bleed? If you can stomach playing a nine cap, you can
play an 11. There's no functional difference beyond the two extra pool,
and you get a step-increase in power.

> If HE loses his Arika to,
> say, not having an Obedience in hand and getting wasted in a rush, that
> deck ends right there. Pentex Subversion? All this can happen to your
> Cailean too. Not a problem, I'd say.

Show me "wasted" in the rule book. It's not there. There's
"burned" which is what PTO does. It burns you. Not kinda, not for a
little while, not until someone comes and yanks you out of it. Toast.

Combat may, if they can climb up that hill, result in burning. It takes a
pile of cards and a lot of luck, something that Arika and a PTO need far
less of. Most often, even on a kick-ass day, it lands your vampire in
torpor. From which you can rescue him. Or your friend can rescue
him. And if neither of those happen, then the offender can take his
*second* minion action and risk *burning himself* to finish the job. You
can do that much more easily with PTO, and even top off your vampire from
the Minion Tap and gain two more pool while you are at it.

Comparing PTO to combat is the most retarded thing in the world. I wish
people would stop.

> Again, that's because everyone plays with small midcaps.

No, it's because very few people can risk participating in such a huge
swing in table balance. I've seen it. I was sitting at a table with some
of the best players in the world not one month ago, the threat of a
cross-table PTO on my Fatima comes out, and suddenly everyone is
scrabbling for one-upsmanship to either make it happen or send it
somewhere else. It is not simply a matter of there being a derth of table
votes.

> So you block with your Cailean, go to long, fire the Mark V, opponent
> play Mayapayatewyrfhewu and Amaranth. He's gone as well. You won't even
> gain 5 pool.

OK, you are looking ridiculous. This is clearly devolved down into a
"well, I play *this*". Sure, the Chimestry-having vampire gets to do some
serious damage at range. And then he burns himself. Maybe good, maybe
dumb. You have just shown how good PTO is, be not requiring one to play
with CHI, or burn oneself, or play with combat cards you are only
marginally likely to use (barring clever exploitation of a
range-strike-heavy metagame).

*Takes a look at the latest EC metagame*

Heck, they'd probably laugh when you influence your Arika out. They'll
laugh even more when you start using her for Governing a Justicar into
play. You guys ARE moving forward no? I mean, we're looking at 4-5 turns
of influencing and doing Govern actions (which are, btw quite easily
blocked) before the deck even becomes a threat. I'm pretty much dead by
then if I'm playing a serious game (aka, not with a
built-to-try-out-a-card fun deck or something). Last time I checked
there aren't an awful lot of tournament winners that used PtO.

To put it simply, decks with big vampires (that can be burned with PtO,
yes) tend not to do very well. I'm sure you can throw up a couple of
examples agianst this, but 4-5-6-7 caps ARE the standard. PtO is JUST
another vulnerability for them. Whether it's really needed or not isn't
the point. I'm all for removing the cross table part, as THAT's the
thing people are complaining about. If you can't stop an action that
kills you, it's your own fault. I can make bleeds for 8 unblockable as
well; haven't seen anyone complain about that.

long as we have to accept the fact that vampires, regardless of their
capacity, all have the same chance of being burned, I don't want to see
PtO changed EXCEPT for the prey-predator clause.

immature and generally biased replies, so IF you decide to reply (the
chance of which I guess at around 90%), try to be a little less biased
and look at it from the other side for once. We ALL hate our vampires
being burned and we ALL hate powerful cards being used against us. Just
because you lost a game or two to PtO doesn't mean it's broken.

closest thing to a broken card atm is DI if you ask me.

decks. In fact, some of the most interesting decks I have seen in the

multi-rush, turbo decks, Omaya walls etc.

Ulugh appears to have some bias against such decks, which I don't fully
understand. It's true that a PTO will significantly hurt that type of
deck much moreso than a weenie-midcap deck, but is there a reason why
this should be the case? If anything, I'd like to see the opposite
effect with weenies and midcaps being the ones targeted, as they start
out with a significant advantage.

Therefore, as another possible change to the card text for PTO. How
about allowing IC members to burn two non-Camarilla vampires below
capacity 6? (ie rather than *any* vampire). I would also add the
condition "once per game". It's still painful, but the selection of
targets becomes much more limited. And one Delaying Tactics will make
the card useless, just like it does for Political Stranglehold etc.

It's not a perfect solution, and I think there may not be a perfect
solution... but this may be preferrable to simply banning the card
altogether.

count

*thematically* to me. I don't think anyone else has mentioned this.

teaming up to lynch and burn a non-Cammie vampire. Fair enough, but
can't this already be done using say Haven Uncovered and Burning Wraths
(or whatever) ?

A vote like Anathema seems much more realistic in its relationship to
combat/burning. It doesn't actually do the deed; it just sets up
conditions for other vampires to do it. That seems more appropriate
somehow. Vampires with lots of influence using said influence to arrange
a vampire's death.

But PTO is like making a combat card that says "Strike: Bleed your prey
for 5". It's just wrong.

about

the

be broadened to include other cards than just PTO...

broken, I do agree that some of them are problematic and should be
changed or banned. Or something anyway.

When someone rushes and kills my vampire, it hurts my game but
ultimately I am still having fun. When someone bleeds me out, I have no
problem offering a handshake in congratulations. When someone PTO's my
vampire, I feel robbed. Maybe not a definition of broken, but still.

have been using PTO. Whether it wins or not is immaterial to whether it
is an unfair card or not. I've seen plenty of times when a PTO has
destablized a table but not actually garnered a win for the PTO'er. Same
thing with Baltimore Purge and Anarch Revolt by the way.

I personally do not equate winning with broken. While not synonymous,

as

their
> > capacity, all have the same chance of being burned, I don't want to

they were sick of being abused by elders with too much power (more or

I've had vampires burned in combat hundreds of times. Is combat broken?

I've had my one-trick-pony Howler burned by a single cross-table PTO. Is

Most definitely:Monocle of Clarity in its original version.

In my experience many people tend to find cards are broken if:
* they get ousted because of it once too often, and get frustrated.
*they see what a certain card can do when played well by a good player
*they see what a certain card can do in certain circumstances, but
fail to grasp the specific factors that enabled it being played that
way, and how small the odds were of it actually doing that.
*they fail to understand how to play against this specific card
*fail to anticipate it being played frequently.
*do not grasp it's weaknesses
*fail to see the difference between a "broken card", and the supremacy
of the player/deckbuilder handling it

IMHO, none of the above reasons make a card broken.
Also IMPO, the closest things this game even has to a broken card are
Deflection/Tel. Misdirection, and even then only by virtue of the
impact they have on tournament play,which I believe to be due to the
lack of (something that remotely resembles)an equivalent in the whole
range of other disciplines or disciplineless cards.So not strictly
because of what the cards do, as I find their specific use an
absolutely necessary factor in the game.

> Sacrifice.

Only works on Sabbat vampires with capacity below 7 belonging to the
same clan as the vampire that's calling the vote. That's a hell of a
lot more restrictions.

> MASTER:
> Society of Leopold.

Great card; but require more than just this to burn a full, large non-
cam vampire.

> And there are other non-combat ways to send vampires to torpor:
>
> Baltimore Purge
> Kiss of Ra
> Legacy of Power
> Nosferatu Performance Art

Torpor != burned.

> ... or by inflicting damage to them outside combat (Shadow Twin,
> Abyssal Hunter, etc.)

Requires more than a single action.

> > 1) Block the action.
> > 2) Have more votes.
>
> There are other "adequate" defenses such as:
>
> Kindred Coercion

Which sucks.

> Pulling Strings

Also sucks. Irregular Protocol is far better.

> Dread Gaze

Sucks.

> Delaying Tactics (yes it is very adequate, although it "just" delays PTO
> one turn).

The only one of two good vote defense cards. Vox Domini is the other.

> In addition, why should I include cards against Immortal Grapple, or heavy
> combat in my decks?

Because combat is a fairly common archetype. And combat != PtO. Combat
may or may not burn a vampire (some decks don't care if you burn, they
just want you in torpor), but they REQUIRE MORE THAN A SINGLE CARD TO DO
IT. And the defenses are much more robust.

> Why do people underestimate defense against political decks). The cards to
> defend you against such decks are there for you to use. If you do not
> use them, it's your problem. Note that they are not only useful against PTO,
> but against Banishment, KRC, Parity Shift, etc. as well.

Because they (for the most part) suck. Dread Gaze is countered by
playing a Bewitching Oration. Kindred Coercion doesn't work on Inner
Circle members (or large vampires in general) unless you're playing one
of your own. Pulling Strings is weaker than Irregular Protocol (and
requires DOM to be remotely useful). And the opportunity cost for all
of them is surprisingly high. Bleed defense is almost always good
because you're almost guaranteed to be bled over the course of a game,
even if no "bleed" decks are on the table (even if it's just for 1).
Combat defense is good because you can almost always get into combat
over the course of a game, even if there are no combat decks on the
table (get blocked or block an action). Vote defense isn't good because
you may not get hit with any votes worth stopping. And even if you do
and have the proper cards, they may not _work_. Pulling Strings and
Irregular protocol can stop a single vampire's votes, but they may have
more voters or Ventrue Headquarters, etc. Or they can just let that
vote fail and call another one. I have yet to see a Kindred Coercion
actually work.

> There are several strategies to win in V:TES. One of them is politics,
> so why not should you include vote defense in your deck? Because
> you prefer to deal with combat, or bleed? ;-)

How often do you actually put Pulling Strings in a deck?

--
-Snapcase

If I have a bunch of Obediences and Majesties in my deck and happen to
have non combat predators and preys, those cards are also useless. Of
course people pack combat defense according to the metagame, and I can't
see why you can't do that with politics. For weenie politics, a single
Suprise Influence early on can totally ruin their deck. Dread Gaze comes
a far way to stop many votes, especially if there's multiple titles on
the table. Sure, if it's done to you crosstable and nobody votes in your
favor, you're pretty much fucked, which is why I'd like it top be
prey/pred only.

that pack like 3-4 majesties and 2 obediences. If they happen to be prey
of a potence rush, they're fucked. If you can't deal with PtO, you also
can't deal with Parity Shify, KRC, Cons Agi, Domain Challenge and every
other vote that screws you. What do you do when you have a Nos Prince
Zillah/Parity deck sitting behind you? Correct. Nothing except maybe
hope your grandprey eases your pain. With not way to stop his votes,
you'll be dead pretty soon. PtO just happens to be a very powerful vote
card, given the correct circumstances, just like Mayapayaterfhdi is a
very strong combat card IN THE RIGHT SITUATION. To many decks, PtO isn't
THAT much different from Sensory Deprivation and yet that card has NO
restrictions. I'm sure you can give me like 10 examples where still
having the vampire, be it unable to act is better than losing it. I
agree, which is why Sens Dep has no restrictions at all and is Directed.
Making PtO only able to target prey and predator would put it, IMO, on
par with Sens Dep.

> How often do you actually put Pulling Strings in a deck?

Never. Because I couldn't care less about that PtO in a friendly game.
If they keep abusing it, they'll get ganged up upon pretty quick. In
tournaments being able to bounce that bleed for 5 is more important that
the remote chance my vamp will be burned by PtO. That, plus tournies
tend to be bleed heavy, so bleed defense is far far more important that
vote defense if you intend to at least reach the finals.

Maybe we DO need a more adequate vote defense card. Or at least one
that's more versatile (much like that new card from Black Hand that
gives 2 votes or +2 bleed). Banning or ruining PtO is not a solution.

vampire back. You have no such chance with PtO.

Case closed.

We've gotten an excellent vote defense card in the last set. But you
can only play 1 per game. Some more versatile vote defense probably
couldn't hurt. But it may or may not stop PtO consistently. They only
have to get 1 through.

I also think that this card has become less strong with the most recent
expansions. Life in the City, Corporal Reservoir, and maybe The Coven,
since it is now more common than it was. I suspect also that Hunting
Grounds are more commonly played than in the past. All these cards will
let a vampire escape the burning effect of Society of Leopold and
possibly transfer it to someone else, which makes SoL a risky
proposition. I still play with it, but I'm a lot more nervous about it
than I used to be.

> There are no cards which are useful against political decks, other
than
> blocking the action or having more votes. Or beating up the vampires
> before they can call the votes.

Which seems fair to me, since most vote decks do require a lot of setup.
Most vote decks seem to me to have a potent ousting method but also tend
to be very fragile. So their strength is appropriately balanced by their
weakness. I play a lot of vote decks, and the card I am always most
afraid of is Immortal Grapple. Much moreso than Delaying Tactics.

In fact, I would say that for most vote decks, Immortal Grapple may be
the best anti-vote card available :)

> Because there is no adequate defense other than blocking the action or
> having more table votes yourself.

Do you feel that there should be better ways available to counter votes?
It seems the designers agree judging by Black Hand, but I'm not sure how
effective the new cards are for this.

Vox Senis is interesting, but inferior to Direct Intervention. And
putting it into play (rather than discarding it) is putting far more
trust in the competency of the other players than I am often prepared to
do.

There are plenty of methods to stop votes, but most of them require so
much focus that they are simply not worth it. I mean, having an
Irregular Protocol, Delaying Tactics, Kindred Coercion and Vox Senis in
your hand will stop even the most determined vote decks. But if you have
4 cards in your hand to stop a vote, that's 4 cards that you're not
using to oust someone. This is much less cost-effective than stopping a
bleed with a single Deflection or stopping a rush with a single
Obedience.

Cheers,
WES

I would have to agree with the arguement that if PTO was widely
availible to all 10 caps then it would be vastly broken. As it is now
there are only 7 vampires in the game that can use it at full power.
In fact, if it was widely availible to 10+ caps, I don't think that a
reasonable cost could be placed on it. Could you imagine the havoc
that would occur if Augustus Giovanni could use it and then
Daemonically Possess the burnt vampire back under control. No pool
cost would be appropriate as you could just blast vampires out of
existance and then bring them back under your control.

The real problem as I see it probably isn't that an IC member can
blast 60% of the vampires out of existance, but rather that Dimple, a
2-cap Nosferatu, can declare himself Nosferatu Justicar and then start
tossing these around the table at the understrength version. That is
where PTO truely makes its mark.

It grossly defies the bleed/bleed defence, combat/combat defence,
politics/political defences that the game is based upon. Even if you
bleed me for 8, if I have managed my pool properly I will survive, or
if you enter combat with me and knock myself into torpor then I can
rescue myself, and political cards which have a high opportunity cost
tend to be more powerful even with Political Flux, or Kindred
Restructure (which I have problems with) you still don't actually lose
"purchased" resources.

PTO on the other hand infact denies you the basics that separate this
game from Magic. Specifically, I am talking about land denial. In
Magic, if you are not able to play a land on your first turn, then in
effect you lose. VTES on the other hand does not have lands. VTES
has transfers. PTO can effectively deny you your first three turns of
transfers which is in effect putting you three turns behind the rest
of the table. You lose. It is a one card trump. It is broken.

Comments Welcome,
Norman S. Brown, Jr
XZealot
Archon of the Swamp

An IC is vampire
Sarah Brando, Jimmy Dunn and Victor Tolliver are a vampire

An IC can hunt, block, bleed

An IC can play an action a turn, the gang can play three

vampires non camarilla with capacity less than 6.

And nothing else, certainly no stupid "once per game". As if embrace
or thin-blood seer could be played only once per game.

Once again, show me thenumerous PtO winning decks.

> non-sabbat, Regent burn an non-sabbat. Not sure how the indy clans
> would get it (and it would only be a settite card anyway, as I still
> haven't managed Ravnos vote.)

It's a lot harder to get a Regent (Sabbat War rare) in play than it is to
get an Inner Circle member in play. I used to have this Goratrix gets
Regent deck...well, best not to bring that disaster up.

> Keeping in mind however, that the Camarilla (when PTO was printed)
> relied upon the titles and politics to keep parity with the sabbat,
> which had all the good vampires. That's why we see Parity Shift v.
> Transfer of Power. 5th v. Blood Feast. PTO v. Sacrifice. etc.

Protect Thine Own was printed in Ancient Hearts, before any Sabbat
vampires were in print (and while independents were still mostly crap,
especially the larger ones). Seems like at the time it was printed it was
a lot less disruptive. Anyone influencing Patrizia Giovanni into play is
going to lose, PTO or no. :)

By the way, in my estimation Parity Shift is a LOT stronger than Transfer
of Power. I do agree that the Sabbat often have better vampires, but that
doesn't necessarily make up for the strength of Protect Thine Own vs. the
trick-deck-only Sacrifice or all-powerful Parity Shift vs. virtually
unplayed Transfer of Power.

But back to the point I was making, it doesn't seem like the designers of
Protect Thine Own intended for the card to be able to burn 2/3 of all
printed vampires since only a small minority of vampires (many of them
quite bad) were vulnerable to it at the time of original printing. That
suggests brokenness, I think.

> I'm perfectly willing to see an increase in the cost of PTO (a pool
> cost seems appropriate) but there are other similiar cards available.
> They aren't as good, just like no card in the game is as good as
> Govern the unaligned. But I still maintain that for PTO to really
> work you have to have a big combo on top of good seating (non-Cam
> prey, PTO, Stealth, Vote push, pool gain, combat defense.) It isn't
> as easy as people are making it seem (and its likely more powerful
> than I am willing to admit.)

Agreed that PTO isn't a sure game winner. What it is though, and the
reason I think people dislike it so much, is a sure game loser for anyone
basing a deck on a large non-Cam vampire. Adding a pool cost to PTO
wouldn't make much difference, IMO, although it would be harder to run a
deck with 14 of them.

The DC playgroup doesn't toss around much PTO. I think that's because
we're all somewhat fond of running large non-Cam vampires (Lazverinus,
Sascha Vykos, Spider Killer, Ankla Hotep, Nu, Synesios and many others
have made appearances in recent games). Let that genie out of the bottle
and we'll all suffer a bit. That also suggests brokenness.

Matt Morgan

to deal with combat, bleed, intercept, etc.

the game. It requires an 8-11 cap to play out of the gate or set up
to call a justicar vote. It requires ways to pass the vote to burn,
ways to call the vote sucessfully, ways to protect your vampire, and
ways to oust after you've called it. You can deal with the table if
you see it. You can deal with the caller if they'll let you (let me
oust this camarilla deck in front of me and I'll roll to you.) You

undercosted. Hard to play well. But not broken.

Which decks are those? I'm more familiar with 8 Majesties being the
staple, and far many more copies of Obedience than you could sanely play
with any other card, specifically *because* the opportunity cost is low

What I mean is that when you compare the three different legs of the V:tES

stopped with a Deflection (stopped for *you* anyway) and a rush is countered
by Obedience among other cards. But a vote deck is to my mind harder to stop
and requires more resources available to do so.

It's true that the same could be said for some defenses against bleed or
combat also. I could be hoarding intercept and wakes for bleeds or
maneuvers, FOR prevention cards for combat etc.

But it's much easier to keep a Deflection ready than it is enough cards to
*stop* a PTO. Delaying Tactics, as has been mentioned, only delays the
inevitable. And yet DT is still considered the best vote defense by most
people. If a vote deck is stopped by a single Irregular Protocol, than I
have to ask how good that vote deck really is.

Now, keep in mind that I don't play a very reactive game generally. I want
all *seven* of the cards in my hand to be ousters, directly or indirectly.
The best counter against most types of decks IMO is to oust them before they
get their engine going.

Cheers,
WES

If I really want to maximize my chances of winning ... in other words,
SERIOUSLY play to win, not play to win with a cool deck that uses a new
idea ... then I must remove as much variance as possible from my deck,
and then tune it for consistent offensive performance. Most defense is
unreliable -- the game is balanced so that offense will always beat out
defense, and that is a good thing, as the game must end at some point.

Though the chances of it happening to me are low by virtue of players'
deck choices, the card will cause me to lose if it is played -- a huge
variance swing. Since I can be sure that at least one deck in any
serious tournament will include PTO (and probably more), to MAXIMIZE my
chances, I must not even give it the opportunity to affect me. This
rules out any non-Cam vampires above 7.

Baltimore Purge's existence adds more fuel to this, though now I need to
include all vampires above 7 as well; while my smaller guys could well
get Grave Robbed, the odds of my having another vampire up to defend
against this are high, as well as just plain having other vampires to
use in case one goes away.

Note that combat hasn't even entered into the equation yet. There are
plenty of ways for big guys to defend themselves in combat, and some big
guys (Lazverinus, Cailean, Goratrix) are much nastier in combat than any
little wannabe Rusher could ever be. But I can't possibly build enough
combat defense AND enough PTO/BP defense into my deck, even if we remove
the possibility that someone will use it cross-table. Many people
choose to simply include only the combat defense, banking on the fact
that combat will be more likely seen than PTO/BP. However, the only
logical answer to maximise one's winning chances is simply to not allow
those cards to affect your game in a significant way, by not
constructing your deck in such a fashion.

I'm not talking about "win every game". I'm talking about maximizing
your chances. Sure, big-vamp decks have won in the past and will do so
in the future. But way, WAY more well-built big-vamp decks have lost
than won... something I believe everyone on the newsgroup tends to
forget when discussing what archetypes do well and what don't.

That was the problem with the card. You either played Deflection or AI

hand, because SOMEONE was going to be using the Big Kaboom.

>broken, but did it win every single game? Didn't people play with
>Deflections or Archon Investigations back then? Seems like bouncing a
>bleed of 14 to one's prey is a sure ticket to VPsville.

One round of a tournament, in a 5 player, every player at my table was ousted
with The Return to Innocence. Wasn't always the prey of the person bleeding
with it. I vaguely recall having double digit pool, maybe as much as 14, when
I was ousted with one or two bleeds.

Responding to something else in this thread, namely the reason for playing
bleed defense and/or combat defense in much greater proportion to vote defense,
I looked at the 2003 winners in the TWDA recently and I don't want to go
through every deck again to make sure about the precise numbers, but roughly:
There are 114 decks.
I count 25 that vote.

I believe around 2 of the decks can reasonably oust without calling votes and
without bleeding. That would leave 87 decks that will definitely bleed and
some more that will bleed as well as vote.

One in four and a half decks sounds low. Because these are only winning decks,
the actual play environment may see a lot more vote decks.

Bottom line: vote defense has a much higher opportunity cost than bleed
defense. This is, BTW, why I'm likely to run DIs for vote defense over DT;
they can always be used for something besides vote defense.

> I think that if you make a broken effect only happen once per game, it's
> still broken and now it's just a race to see who gets to the broken

Just chiming in late--yeah, making the card only playable once per game
wouldn't make the effect less broken (as it is way broken), but it at least
would be a very easy, very precidented fix that would successfully make the
card much less of an issue. If it is only playable once per game, you only
can reasonably put so many in a deck, meaning it is unlikely to come up
much, and it makes something like Delaying Tactics and DI much more of a
viable defense (assuming that if it gets delayed or DIed, it still counts as
being "played").

now it rarely ever comes up, 'cause it was given the "Once per game" limit.
And Temptation was much less damaging than PTO (at least you got some pool
in exchange...).

Messages.Author: Azel
Messages.Body:
hmm, i was sitting here thinking about how this card represents the
Camarilla taking on vampires as an entire sect to get rid of a single
opposing vampire. thematically wouldn't this mean that the Camarilla has
instituted some sort of eternal bum-rush against the said minion until they
are ash? If so why doesn't Protect Thine Own represent some of the casualty
factor of this?

Perhaps keeping the original effect of the entire card but increase its cost
by requiring the player to sacrifice enough of his own vamires (burnt into
the ash heap mind you) up to the capacity cost of targeted vampire - and any
excess capacity over gets converted into pool. This way ICs can trade off
for big 11-caps, showing the idea that it was a major battle and both ended
up dying. Or having 3 or so mid-caps being burnt off to destroy a big cap,
showing that the casualty rate is intense.

This is probably an overly penalizing effect. But I feel it's thematic. Also
it keeps a hoser card from being reduced to nullity (like being banned or
"one referendum per game"). I believe that the Camarilla's big power of
organization and voting needs to be represented in the game. It needs to
hose opposition. I like well designed clan/sect hoser cards - it makes the
card world reflect the flavor of the world it represents. That I believe is
some of the great charm of V:tES, all the clans/sects and hostile
interaction.

But that said PTO is far too powerful as it stands and represents no real
struggle for said effects. I believe the obscene hosing effect can be kept,
but the opportunity cost as a simple action (which is undeniably obscene as
it stands) needs to be representatively increased. If you had to sack a
Justicar, IC member, or some other combination of vampires equivilent to the
capacity to get rid of a horrifying non-Cam would you do it so flippantly?
Or would you really think hard about it? It'd still see play this way and
yet also show that the might of the Camarilla is in unity and organization,
not sheer brute force.

Too harsh? Too weak? how would you tweak this idea?

On Mon, 5 Jan 2004, Ulugh Beg II wrote:

> I'm not asking for anything. It's just that you (and several other
> people) keep redefining the problem with PtO to counter arguments in
> favor of it.

I'm not redefining it. I think PTO is broken in about half a dozen
ways. As you make some argument against it's brokenness, I will naturally
point to the aspect that I feel refutes it. It's not shifting the
goalpost, it's carrying on a multi-faceted discussion (for the millionth
time).

> First the pool loss is the problem. So, PtO-pro suggest that half the
> pool is regained.

Of course, that's admitting the card needs changing. Then it's just
haggling as to how. Personally, I've never wavered from my position that
it should just be flat-out banned. I'll counter-argue various
justifications for not banning it, but that's my take.

> Then all of a sudden it's the actual minionloss that's
> the problem. Of course any analogy to combat, banishment or Sens dep is
> simply ignored or called "not the same thing" without further arguments.

No, it's called not the same thing without typing out the same thing I
typed out yesterday, all over again. Really, did I just hallucinate and
imagine that I talked once about how SenseDep is very different, much
weaker, and more balanced than PTO? Ditto for combat? I only dismiss it
because I've already made the argument. Or someone has, and I'm not
repeating them.

> Then the problem is that big vamps are already too weak anyway and that
> PtO fucks up just those decks, while those decks should be improved with
> or without changing PtO anyway. And now all of a sudden fatties are
> perfectly competitive. Make up your mind.

It's an unfair advantage for the Camarilla. It makes fatties, already
difficult to play at the highest level, even more so. What more reason do
you need? In either case, it isn't an either/or scenario.

> > > What is it? Is it so overpowered that it scares non-cam fattie decks
> > > away on tours? (but it apparently doesn't?? wtf)

Some people have balls. They're usually stupid for displaying them, as
some Einstein who thinks his Dom/Obf bleed deck is the height of skill
walks away with the victory, but they have them all the same.

> I didn't say that. I merely stated that big vampires are too weak in
> general to be competitive, aside from a few trick decks.

And wouldn't it be nice to rectify that, just a little. Not grab the
pendulum and bury it in the wall on the other side, just..... even things
out a little bit. Are you wedded to the status quo.?

> The term
> useless, I think I used, was merely a word I copied from a previous post
> to make clear what line I was replying to. You, of course, pick just
> that to, well, pick on.

Well you used the word. Don't blame me for not knowing you actually meant
something other than what you wrote.

> You really can't disagree that playing with
> fatties is far riskier than with midcaps or weenies and require more
> than just deckbuilding and play skill to win with.

No, of course not. The game is heavily slanted towards weenie vampires
and Camarilla vampires. Wouldn't it be nice if it weren't so? Imagine
that you had the power to do something about it. Imagine there was some
guy who decides what gets changed in the game, and that he might be
listening. Fantasy, I know, because if there were such a guy, he'd
obviously be sipping rum out of coconuts and fucking dark-skinned women on
some tropical island with his pilez of mad loot, not spending all his time
lurking on some newsgroup. But just imagine.....

> As far as I know the ONLY argument I've seen against PtO is that it's
> "too strong" or "stupid that it can't target cams" or "it means game
> over for certain decks".

Those are three good arguments. Do you think they are wrong, or do you
think they are right, but just need even more reasons. Because if it's
the former, I'm going to say "see previous posts." If it's the latter,
we're done, cause you are nuts. Well, the last one *could* be a bad
argument, but it actually isn't.

> The IMO is pretty critical in this argument. You do believe it's too
> strong. I don't, considering the restrictions. Of course these
> restrictions are "no problem at all" and yet 4 card rush combo's are
> "out of the discussion". All the while we're playing PtO, Elder
> Impersonation, Forgotten Labyrinth AND Bewitching Oration. All with
> Arika, who is soooo easy to get and keep on the table, of course.

It is sooooo easy to get, watch: I transfer 11. I have Arika. Keeping is
quite a bit easier. Obedience goes 99% of the way. But the real fallacy
here is wishing to keep calling this PTO thing a 4 card combo. It
isn't. +1 stealth, 5 votes in favor. Sure, some tables are title-fests,
but those titles are as likely to be for you as against you, as you deal
for the votes (like, I call the next one on some guy you don't like), or
you target some combat god that any non-combat god wants to see gone, etc
etc). Table votes are exactly a wash, and therefore not a
consideration. You play with push anyway, but that has more to do with
fueling your minion tap and taking free +1 stealth actions that say "Gain
two pool, and..... stuff." Then there are the tables where having the
edge is vote lock, and those tables happen. They even happen in good
groups. Don't try to tell me otherwise. So, the votes you have, you
start with stealth. Who starts with intercept? A negligible number of
vampires. After that, it's a card-for-card tit-for-tat. One card, PTO,
burns the vampire. There is no one card that does that in combat. Heck,
you ate up one card just getting there, in all likelihood.

> There's multiple cards that target only Sabbat, Cammies, Indeps or a
> certain clan. Whether or not this is a good idea in the first place has
> nothing to do with how broken PtO is.

And that's fine. That's variety. The magnitude of PTO's effect,
*combined* with it's exclusivity and scope, are the combinant problem.

Yes, there's the real kick in the pants. "Non-Camarilla".

What would you feel about PTO reading "if this vampire is an Inner
Circle member, then choose any vampire". Remove the restriction from
not being able to burn Camarilla vampires...

Restricting it from targeting the Camarilla vampires merely limits
deck options. Why not give every clan/sect the same fear of PTO.
There's no reason that the cammies should get off the hook (since
there's no "non-independant" and "non-Sabbat" PTO). All that does is
limit deck construction.

People that like the card as it is should have no problem with the
above change; it will balance the card away from being a sect hoser
and towards just being a vampire hoser. It won't be a limiting factor
on deck construction anymore, since there will be no specific
disadvantage for playing large non-cam vamps instead of large Cam
vamps. People that hate the card because they continually get their
big non-cam vampires burned won't have a change of argument. And
they'd get to see the love spread out a bit.

Get on the bandwagon now! Sign the petition for the PtO upgrade!

--

Easy as pie. Current card text on Sacrifice:

Political Card-Worth 1 Vote.
Called by any Sabbat vampire with capacity above 7 at +1 stealth. Choose
a vampire with a capacity below 7 who belongs to the same clan as the
acting vampire. Successful referendum burns the chosen vampire.

---------------------------

Sacrifice is inferior to PTO in the following ways:

1) Cannot burn 7-caps or older. Burning Jost Werner can often be a kick
in the pants for Jost's controller, but 6-caps only cost 6 pool, and
losing one 6-cap is typically not the end of your game for that very
reason -- you'll have other vampires with PRE/AUS.

2) Must be the same clan as the acting vampire. Out of the box, PTO can
affect 397 out of 699 vampires: approximately 56.7% of the vampires in
the game. The Sabbat clans average about 23 vampires each -- so out of
the box, Sacrifice can affect 3.2% of the vampires in the game... but
actually less than THAT even, because it can't affect the 7-caps and up
in each clan.

3) No Inner Circle members in the Sabbat -- can't get 4 votes in favor
without a Regent card.

---------------------------

Sacrifice is superior to PTO in the following ways:

1) Doesn't cost a blood.

2) Doesn't require a title.

---------------------------

It doesn't take a genius to see the scales are heavily weighted in PTO's
favor. Sure, we've all seen Malkavian Antitribu decks drop Deranges on
people and then Sacrifice them, but you still can't get past
disadvantage #1 with a Derange -- and !Malks don't have PRE as an
in-clan discipline.

Should Sacrifice exist? No, it's a generic clan-hoser and we have all
agreed long ago that clan hosers are basically just dumb. But by the
same token, it's far from broken, because not only can you not win with
it, you can't even make someone else LOSE without some really contrived
scenarios.

Messages.Author: Curevei
Messages.Body:
>The environment that
>matters is the one where everyone is playing to win, and I would really
>like to see it happen someday... all the good players bringing actual
>STRONG decks, instead of decks that are good-but-creative.
>
>I think we'd find out awful darn quick which cards are broken if people
>really tried.

There are a number of things I prefer about multiplayer CCGs. One of the
things I prefer about two-players is that you can isolate card strength. The
problem with multiplayers is that personality is too often more important than
deck strength, that it's in fact possible that playing a strong deck can work
against you. I find analysis fascinating and it's hard to analyze anything
when any ole crap deck can win simply due to table politics.

I'd find it really interesting to see what happens when "everyone" played (in
some event or series of events) the decks they thought were most powerful and
metagamed against a field that they expected to play the most powerful decks.
Wouldn't necessarily find it all that interesting to play. More relevant to
why I wouldn't expect to see it happen is that I find it less interesting to
try and play such a deck only to play against a mixed field of strong and
not-so-strong decks.

Messages.Author: Azel
Messages.Body:
Oh, i put vote defense in all my decks if i can. it only makes sense - it's
the third main means of ousting your opponents. combat, bleed, vote. yup,
gotta have a little to protect against them all. some focused decks forego
it due to slot restrictions, but i make more toolboxy decks :)

that said i can assure you that vote is a whole other can of fish than bleed
and combat (which it should be naturally). the inherent +1 in each poli
action really strains my intercept which i try to save for combat and bleed,
which in a way i guess it should. the power to damage your prey and
grandprey and king-make reliably through KRCs, Parity Shifts, Reversals of
Fortune, Drastic Upheavals and other though is some serious power. To stave
off stolen VPs i include DTs. And against an emergency i try to include an
irregular protocol (an overdue card by the way).

But the thing is, even with those in hand, maybe an Alamut if assamite, and
maybe a floating 2-vote independent I'm still petrified of voting. it can do
some serious bloating where it can aford to ignore it's predator. i can't
think of many bleed decks or combat decks that can afford to ignore their
predator. but i can't tell you how many times i've seen vote decks literally
ignore the pressure exerted by their predator. bloat and a few obediences or
bounce (all from one discipline by the way) literally nulls the majority of
predators you can face, unless it's a fellow voter.

now yes, there's taste of vitae, provisions of silsila, and other blood
gaining means to minion tap; but bloating for combat is nowhere near the
realm of vote. now, i can forgive this, try to find a way to deal with it,
etc. but what i can't accept is the sheer poor quality of anti-vote cards.
my defenses are all but ignored, along with my assaults. only occasionally
can i snag that teflon elder and attempt to send it to torpor. just torpor!
then it's a whole other prayer to get through the "spare justicar" to
diablerie. and after all that i risk an assured loss of my own minion. sure
sometimes i can get lucky and pull off a weenie potence combat burn - but
don't EVER compare that to the reliability of the referendum. all these
silly block comparisons forget that this same thing can happen to whatever
weenie potence vampire - you just lost sight of your target, just like a
vote can. so let's be sane and call that even. but who here has the guts to
call the REFERENDUM as variable, unpredictable, and evenly balanced as
COMBAT? please, i invite the argument. I have NEVER seen it, please
enlighten me. I WANT, and have been SEEKING, a way to do so.

you think my hard earned counters on alamut can stave this off? haha, well
hasn't yet, but i can hope. has my DT saved me? well for one turn, which
usually just busts out the KRC instead now, and the PTO later. oh how about
the IP? nah, that "spare voting-house" solved that. my 2-vote non-cam? haha,
well that guy's days are numbered if not already piffed away to my ash heap!
no, none of my experience at tables i've played on, or others i was next to
bared out the vagueries of vote

you know what vote gets against this "atrocious" imbalance of combat's
ability to burn their vampires after a lot of work? a vote card that can do
it for them. no, not send to torpor, not to the uncontrolled region, but to
the ash heap. do not pass go, do not collect 200, do not call blood hunt
(which would be a joke anyways). and the kicker? they can keep doing their
bloating thing from this action!!! they can play their game again in all
oblivion that they even had a predator! and this "gift" also furthers
king-making into piffing away without recourse cross table vampires,
preferrably their grand-prey's. you think eagles sight balances this out? i
laugh. now you are asking to make a deck according to your design - should i
make a camarilla vote deck too? yes, yes, that might solve the problem...
diversity is just for whittling away the long winter game nights i see.

True,....perhaps that is a problem, but i have never seen anyone use

As to
> "one man" decks.... If you field a large vampire, how much pool do you

True, more difficult, but not undoable. In the tournaments i played i

tournaments are usually about 20 players big, so i will not be able to
tell what everyone is playing, but an overall estimation of what it
will look like is possible. And you can adjust your decks to the decks
you think will be strong in that envrionment and you will encounter in
the finals.

Yes, PTO is strong, but there are to many requirements to make it
broken.
If we look at the old RtI that was broken in my opinion, you only need
one unblocked (unbounced) action to make someone loose a lot of pool.
...Everyone has pool...and when they lose it you win...
Not everyone has a non-cam-vampire, not everyone loses when they lose
one of their non-cam-vamps, that, on TOP of the fact that it is a VOTE
that can only be called effectively by very little (fragile) vampires
makes it strong, but not broken.

in my opinion.
:-)

I wouldn't have mind if it was made a bit weaker from the start, but i
hate changing cardtexts.

> Does anyone else find it amusing that many of those who are arguing

Yes, I find it interesting. It confirms my impression of some of the
differences between the italio-franco-spanish metagame and the american
one. Of course the sample size is ridiculously small, but my reluctance
to form an opinion is mitigated somewhat by the sheer consistency of
anecdotes. FWIW, here is my general clumping of the metagames, and a
short description of each:

USA: heterogenous; a mix between "serious" and goofy, suggesting that deck
construction is not the prime determiner in who or what wins.

"Old Europe": whatever looks strongest, play it; combat-lite

Scandinavia: like above, but the Toreador have guns.

Brits: fairly combat-heavy; can't be too complicated to play on account of
everyone being hammered.

Australia: gore-fest; critical mass of combat achieved; very interesting
metagame to observe.

South America: can't tell; hear more about Princes, shopowners, and
distributors stealing cards than I do about games.

On 6 Jan 2004, Wouter Kuyper wrote:

> True,....perhaps that is a problem, but i have never seen anyone use
> PTO on an ally. Just doesn't seem like a logical choice. If it indeed
> happens a lot, perhaps that should change. BUt again, i have never
> seen it.

I have. I have been that ally, more than a few times. More often than
that, I've had to somehow *justify* why my "bridge partner" -- who is
playing an IC deck with at least one broken card and, therefore, can
rationally plan a strategy around stomping the table -- shouldn't screw me
with it, and then wonder if I should pound him anyway to keep it from
coming up again next turn. It's. Just. Too. Big. An. Effect.

> Not at all! What i am arguing is that you shouldn't play
> big-noncam-vamps when you expect to see a lot of PTO, or play some
> sort of defense against it.

I should have gotten to this a lot earlier, but lets drop the "one man
deck" term. I don't know of any, except maybe Anson Mastercard Decks,
that are one-vampire affairs. Usually, you sink 8 to 10 into a main
guy, then a few more on some disposable minions. You can't *spend* 9 or
10 on a main guy and have much more than that. You can, but that's a
Governing, parity shifting, minion-tapping, voter capping kind of
thing. There should be more decks playable with large minions than
that. The *possibility* of PTO is a significant deterrent against that.

As for playing defense against it, how much defense do you need to have to
reliably see it, will it make a difference, and what does playing with a
hand size of six or less do to your deck's overall performance in order to
do so? I heard all the "defend against it" arguments before when I was
getting slaughtered in weenie-hell for two years straight. Sure,
defensive cards exist, but even a prominent feature in your metagame isn't
the *only* feature. While you are trying to include your own game *PLUS*
don't-kill-me-wth-your-broken-crap, on the chance that you happen to sit
next to kill-you-with-broken-crap, they have no worries at all, and simply
play kill-you-with-my-broken-crap.

It's just better if there isn't broken crap. More diversity, more
fairness. The only people who object are the ones who get their kicks
winning with it. Find something else to win with. You can do that as
easily as I can tie every non-cam deck I concieve of into pretzels hoping
I don't sit at the same table with you.

> Just as that you should increase the number of obedience when you
> expect to see a lot of rush. Or increase the number of deflections
> when you expect to see a lot of stealth-bleed, or play with more
> Aranthebes when you expect a lot of weenies.

The last one isn't in the same category as the other two, but I won't go
into it. The first two *are* reliable features of any and every game you
play. Opportunity cost. Low. You can play with those cards; you
probably should play with those cards. Bleeding happens. Blocking
happens and, hence, combat happens. As has been stated before, the
defenses against votes, other than blocking the action, are really very
poor. But I do defend against it, to the extent that I play 2 DT's and 2
DI's in most decks. It's still rarely any kind of defense.

> PTO is just a vote, if you expect strong IC-votedecks to come to your
> table, adjust! either to the fact that they are bigvamps (rush?) or to
> the fact that they want to vote (voxes/DI/DT) or to the fact that they
> are IC's (fear of mekhet) or make yourself a more difficult target
> (play cammy) or don't be hurt that much by outspeeding him and putting
> bets on different horses instead of on 1/2 (weenie)
> ... every deck style has its nemesis...

PTO is too much of a nemesis against too many possible decks. That is
part of the issue.

> I would remove the most of the PTO's from my deck if there were not
> enough valuable targets (with my prey or predator). Assuming most
> people adjust their decks according to what they encounter, you can
> play your Thetmes again.

I grasp how metagames develop. Part of the inadequacy of that response is
that you can't really adjust to a tournament metagame. Take for example a
tournament in Washington DC in a few weeks. I might go. It's a four hour
drive. I see those guys a few times a year. Is anything I do or they do
really going to impact our deck choices? What are they even playing
currently? Does that have anything to do with what they'll play at a
tournament?

Rather than all this accomodating, why not just ban the card? IC decks
are still more than, much more than, viable, and a big headache is
removed. Barring self-interest, I just can't see the objection. Sure,
banning is bad, but it's not the end of the world. WW seems to have an
eye on other CCG companies and what works for them. Well, banning cards
has worked fine. The Magic tournament scene hasn't dried up, and they ban
stuff right and left. Few cards need banning. This one does. Ban it.

> True, more difficult, but not undoable. In the tournaments i played i
> usually was able to tell what kind of decks would do well. Those
> tournaments are usually about 20 players big, so i will not be able to
> tell what everyone is playing, but an overall estimation of what it
> will look like is possible. And you can adjust your decks to the decks
> you think will be strong in that envrionment and you will encounter in
> the finals.

You will have to tell me your secret. I have no idea what I'll see at any
given tournament, and other people's potential decks, barring actual
personal knowledge on my part, is never a consideration. I think about
what's strong *in the game* and plan for that. Therefore, I always plan
for PTO.

> Yes, PTO is strong, but there are to many requirements to make it
> broken.

Yeah, play Arika or Alexandria. Don't flip heads eight times in a
row. Real tough.

> If we look at the old RtI that was broken in my opinion, you only need
> one unblocked (unbounced) action to make someone loose a lot of pool.
> ...Everyone has pool...and when they lose it you win...

And unblocked AND unbounced is trivial? Hell of a lot harder than passing
a vote with an IC memeber. Your argument just crumbled to dust.

> Not everyone has a non-cam-vampire, not everyone loses when they lose
> one of their non-cam-vamps, that, on TOP of the fact that it is a VOTE
> that can only be called effectively by very little (fragile) vampires
> makes it strong, but not broken.

IC's are not fragile. That dust is now dust in the wind.

> as easy as people are making it seem (and its likely more powerful
> than I am willing to admit.)

Sure. It's not something that just always makes you win no matter what.
But the effect is ridiculously powerful.

I think Derek's use of the term "unfair" as another useful category
besides "broken" is good here. Protect Thine Own is probably more of an
"unfair" card than a "broken" one. It screws up the game by making its
victim lose, a lot of the time. And it's victimizing them for having
chosen to play large-capacity non-Camarilla vampires. In that way, it's
a lot like getting hosed by clan hosers - except that people actually
play with PTO because unlike clan hosers, they can count on non-Cam
vamps to show up pretty often.

It seems to me, having played with both, that current PTO is a lot like
original Temptation of Greater Power. Both are playable against a wide
range of vampires, but are only severely abusive against high-capacity
vamps. But ToGP got nerfed, and PTO hasn't yet.

On that topic, it's true that applying the ToGP "fix" (playable once per
game) to PTO isn't really a fix of the card's effect. It's still harsh
if it happens and on the flip side it may go too far in making a lot of
copies of PTO not very useful anymore. But what that approach *does*
have going for it is that it's very simple - probably the simplest
card-text change that would accomplish anything, without banning the
card.

Josh

Yes, exactly. Clan hosers are not fair. It's certainly my feeling that
they should never have been created (or at least not with any level of
effect beyond "flavor").

There are a lot of effects that shouldn't exist in VTES regardless of
opportunity cost. Burning vampires without sending them to torpor first
(in combat, preferably) is probably one of them. It's easy to see that
it's possible for high opportunity cost to not be enough to balance a
stronger effect: imagine an action only playable if you have exactly 3
pool and 1 minion in play, and your prey has exactly 20 pool and 4
minions in play. It causes your prey to burn 20 pool. Is that
balanced? Its opportunity cost is astronomical.

In general, it seems to me that there's a certain level of strength that
just shouldn't be surpassed in a single card, no matter how high the
opportunity cost appears. It's simply not appropriate for single cards
to cause that much swing in VTES, even if they're not very easy to play.
I had always believed that this was why Temptation of Greater Power was
changed.

Josh

Yeah, but it was new in Camarilla Edition. That means that you get one

analyze the strongest cards/decks in the game if a lot of the most
experienced players don't find those decks to be the ones they're

main tournament format. Because VTES doesn't do that, there isn't a
continually changing environment to cause the set of "currently best
decks" to evolve substantially over time. It would be a huge pain to do
that like Magic does, for sure, but (at least in theory) it could be
interesting to see if people's interest in building/playing the absolute
strongest possible decks could be maintained that way.

to be safe from it, I have to cut out playing large non-cams. Is that
really how it should be? And indeed, Dave hasn't been arguing for it's
banning in local playgroups; he wants it gone from tournaments.

if we'll ever come up with card text that'll work.

> each one having it's own weaknesses and strengths. Don't hate one
> card because of it's strength, go after it's weakness.

But when going to a tournament (where there's a good deal of people
coming and you don't have some sort of inside knowledge of the metagame)
do you expect PTO? You have no way to tell. So you have to either 1.
ignore the existence of PTO and possibly lose because of it, or 2. limit
your deck choices. It's the limiting of deck choice that I think really
has people up in arms. You can completely ignore PTO if you just play
with a cam vamp instead of a non-cam.

"wolflord" <jo.her...@sca.com> wrote in message
news:88f9561d.04010...@posting.google.com...

> Disagree. There's sadly been this "Aargh Arika!! Must kill on sight"
> hype for the past couple of years which tends to turn the table
> against anyone playing Arika, with or without good reason.People will
> go to absurd lengths to try and wipe Arika off the table, often withot
> even benefitting in the least from this direction of actions..

Wiping Arika out if you can is usually a good move. While wiping out any
vampire out generally works out somewhat well, Arika has 3 bleed, 4 votes,
fortitude for multiple actions and defense, dominate/presence for bloating
(among other things), obfuscate for stealth...her discipline spread is just
far too good to ignore. So while you may disagree, if I'm sitting next to
Arika, I'm generally gonna do what I can to wipe her out.

> > > Delay
> >
> > Fantastic card. They'll do it again next turn.
> No they wont. Not necessarily.Whenever I play tournaments, I always
> include DT and DI's.You can always ask Reyda to testify what the
> effects of that are on political decks being payed at those tables.

Not necessarily, but if the person calling the PTO is not near ousted and
nobody can do anything about the IC calling the vote (the odds of both
conditions being met is relatively high I'd say) then they will most likely
call it again...or oust you with a KRC or something if somehow they got you
into ousting range in the meantime, neither of which I would consider a
favorable option. DT may be a great counter to a VP-stealing Kindred
Restructure (because the point of the Kindred Restructure probably no longer
exists after the current turn) and other such vote tricks, however, it is a
tad less effective in stopping a PTO.

> > >outvote them
> >
> > They start with inherently more votes than any of your single vampires
> > will. Unreliable at best.
>
> Same goes for every single other decent political deck which does not
> include PTO. If your deck is not prepared to handle those, you have a
> different problem alltogether, and then we should stop discussing the
> brokenness of PTO.

I don't see how what you just said has any bearing on the fact that
outvoting a PTO is not very likely, which you seem to agree with. I'm just
curious about what the point of the above statement was, that's all.

> Having the votes is necessary for any vote.
> One of the inherent problems of voting decks (this requires card
> slots).Therefore an inherent problem (weakness )of playing PTO. q.e.d.

Perhaps it can be considered an inherent weakness that you need the votes,
however, this weakness is relatively insignificant. With an IC and the vote
card, that's already five votes in favor. This may not outvote every table
in existance, however, just one bewitching oration (which you're probably
using for the bloat aspect anyway) pushes that up to nine (assuming the IC
has PRE, not all IC's have PRE, but if you're playing a vote deck you're
probably using PRE at the very least for voter caps if not also BOs and
other such cards.) If nine votes still isn't enough (which may be true
later in the game, certainly not at the beginning) you probably have other
titled vampires out to at the very least help you pass your votes. Passing
votes doesn't require an excessive amount of card slots in every vote deck.
Sure it still takes up some card slots, but as I mentioned above, some of
those vote push cards also serve as bloat anyway, which is generally good.

> More than half the vampires in the game are legal targets.
> That doesn't mean "more than half the vampires you'll ever see in a
> decent game".
> This logic does not make sense, as the number of legal targets
> "existing in the game" has no direct connection to the number of
> targets you'll find in a given game, on a given table.

No it doesn't, but it does increase the chance you'll see a valid target in
the game. Because it can affect a greater variety of targets, it makes it a
more flexible card than if it were just a clan hoser.

> > If you lose the 10 cap your deck is designed around, when your
> > predator has an IC member behind you, I'd say you're pretty screwed,
> > barring extreme luck.
>
> If your deck is based on 1 10 cap, then I'd say you've designed a deck
> that will have trouble dealing with an overwhelming majority of other
> decks.
> You're complaining about the difficulty of playing decks that are
> based on 1 high cap here, not about the power of PTO.In your opinion,
> do you think Pentex Subversion is broken as well?

As a note, a deck based on one ten-cap vampire will more than likely have
support weenies out. Support weenies can get rid of Pentex. Support
weenies can block rushes. Support weenies can do lots of things to help out
big fattie. Support weenies most likely can't do much about a PTO (yes,
they can DT it, but I still question the effectiveness of DT in stopping PTO
cold.)

> > Eliminating your prey's cornerstone vampire doesn't help you oust
> > them? I'd love to see the decklists of decks designed around large
> > non-Cam vamipres that are this impervious to PTO.
>
> *possibly* eliminating his cornerstone
> If you succeed, it *might* *help* you, or not, or something in
> between. It might just as well turn the table on you.Again, it doesn't
> oust people by itself.See more about my opinion on decks based on
> cornerstone vamps above.

Old Thoughts Betrayed wasn't an assured way to victory. Old Majesty didn't
guarantee victory either. I also don't see how old Form of Mist on its own
was assured to help. The list of changed cards that didn't assure victory
in their old forms goes on and on. Generally, no card ousts people by
itself, but some cards are powerful enough to just be too powerful.

> Also, I'd like to add, I keep finding it so bizar that you're actually
> looking at it as if it were the Camarilla as a sect who have access to
> this card. This is an incorrect idea. It's the IC's who do, and to a
> lesser amount/effect the justicars. These are individual vamps, not
> the sect as such.Sect as such actually has absolutly nothing to do
> with it. By this logic, I don't see why you would create a card
> requiring the other sects as such,rather a vampspecific card for
> certain titled vamps..
> Unless of course you guys pay strictly single sect crypted decks??

If a card requires a titled vampire from that sect, I'd consider it a sect
card. Sure not all Camarilla vampires can use it, however, in order to use
the card you MUST be playing at least one Camarilla vampire. I suppose the
definition of whether or not a card is a sect card if it requires a titled
vampire of that sect is up for debate, however, I don't think I'm alone when
I say that it is reasonable to say that if it requires a titled vampire of
that sect, it can be considered a card for that sect.

Now, I'm not sided either way with the broken or not broken crowds, although
when I see the card I think "Sheesh, that's nasty." Not nasty in a Govern
the Unaligned way, where it's good and powerful, but nasty in the "Man, I
don't even feel like playing this card because it can quite easily ruin
people and the game" way.

Messages.Author: David Cherryholmes
Messages.Body:
On Wed, 7 Jan 2004, Tetragrammaton wrote:

> In my experience, discarding is ok, but in a vote deck
> (the typical in which i see PTO used) 2 or 3 vote cards to be discarded
> being useless means much.

What's being got at is the opportunity cost of including the card in your
deck. Clan hosers are not often played because the odds of it just
sitting in your hand and clogging things up is high. Pitching a vote is
strong; while it's only one vote, it has a bit of a wildcard effect, and
I've seen it cause big changes in a game. The fact that you can use PTO
in this fashion at a minimum means the opportunity cost is, in fact,
low. Coupled with the fact that it just takes one to wreck many decks,
and put many others on the ropes, well..... you know the drill.

> I will never risk to put in more that 3 PTO in any vote deck, since i simply
> don't want to take the risk of cloggin my hand thereafter,

But the risk is low. If a vote is called, you can play it. If diablerie
happens you can play it. Barring all that, as a last resort, you can
discard it. The hyper-focused crowd may view being forced to discard
anything at all as a failure, I don't know, but I don't view the
occasional discard as any great burden, especially when the bulk of your
activity will be consumed with tier 1 effects.

On 7 Jan 2004, wolflord wrote:

> Disagree. There's sadly been this "Aargh Arika!! Must kill on sight"

> against anyone playing Arika, with or without good reason.People will
> go to absurd lengths to try and wipe Arika off the table, often withot

Not in my experience, at least not with good players. Sure, when she
comes out there'll be moaning and bitching and comments about that
player's personal hygiene, but in reality people keep their eye on the
ball, their prey and predator. Sure, you've got to keep an eye on Arika,
because she can blow out 12+ pool in one go, so if your predator is in
that range, you might have to get pre-emptive. Note that this goes to the
heart of the problem, though, because from the other side of the fence,
that same offensive power means the Arika player is even more likely to
pre-emptively strike with the PTO just before wrapping around. The fact
is, Arika gets no help. Luckily she doesn't need it. And that's about
it.

> You pay 1 third of your starting pool. You risk getig ousted before
> you even get your vamp into play. They had better bring you something
> extr, for all that effort.

Right, big vampires are risky, despite the fact that Arika has many ways
to almost immediately recoupe that pool or obviate the need to actually
spend any more (govern down - freak - Enchant down - freak - scout down -
freak - restore - freak - bleed - freak - vote - push - cap, mix in
restoration as needed). Of course that's a ridiculously long chain of
cards, but they are all cards that will exist in multiples in the deck (or
most likely should), and even small chunks of the combo on any given turn
pretty much refute your assertion. But even stipulating that you are
correct, why should it be *so* much riskier to play large non-cam than
cam. Keep your eye on the ball. The real issue isn't that PTO can't be
defended against; it can be, simply by playing small vampires or cam
vampires. The real issue is that it makes a wide range of decks a dumb
decision to play, and this harms the game as a whole.

> It does not *have*to be mentioned. I don't undertand why people wil
> simply not acept this cxard as being a truly important (necessary)
> part of the game. It was IMHO introduced exactly to create an overall
> defens..
