it" argument, then the card is a problem. Anything can be DI'd. Here,
watch: hypothetical card says "+1,000 stealth action -- DIE!". Just DI
it, right?

> No they wont. Not necessarily.Whenever I play tournaments, I always
> include DT and DI's.You can always ask Reyda to testify what the
> effects of that are on political decks being payed at those tables.

DT doesn't stop the card. It delays it. It's been said many times. See
above for DI. And yes, I understand that, in the time you buy, you *may*
be able to do something about it. Or you may not. None of this addresses
the fact that the card does more than one card should do, nor that it is
only a factor for non-cams.

> Same goes for every single other decent political deck which does not
> include PTO. If your deck is not prepared to handle those, you have a
> different problem alltogether, and then we should stop discussing the
> brokenness of PTO.

Magnitude of effect. One vote, generate 3-5 pool loss for a
player. Losing three to five pool happens in all kinds of ways, and is
something everyone has to account for. Tactical nukes from orbit are
something only non-cams have to account for. Were it not of "tactical
nuke" magnitude, it wouldn't be a problem.

> weakness?

Burned out. Somebody else will re-re-re-re-state this one.

> I'll gladly play anyone who plays PTO according to this logic..

that a player can assess the impact on table balance and choose
accordingly? You guys are masters of stealth bleed in Paris? Well, I'm a

> between. It might just as well turn the table on you.Again, it doesn't
> oust people by itself.See more about my opinion on decks based on

broken", which is a fallacious argument.

Messages.Author: Ulugh Beg II
Messages.Body:
> Is it really a given? I have heard that the european players take the
> game very seriously and are in a sort of permanent cantankerous state
> because of it. There has to be some difference between competetiveness
> and emotional involvement.

I think you're confusing competitive with competitive here. Or I am.
Whatever. I'll explain.

> Perhaps your comment was not limited to vtes. I take it as a given
> that americans are far more competitive at basketball than europeans.

No doubt that in MANY MANY sports the US has the best player(s) and the
tougest opposition. Fairly simple, it's the bigger landmass, produces
tons of people and logically has the most talent around. That, however,
has nothing to do with playing style. Also, basketball is in the US as
soccer is here in Europe, so your example was pretty bad in this case.
Take an international game like Tennis or Swimming and we're talking.

What I'm merely saying, is that for all its size, the US still doesn't
dominate every competition. Statistically it should, simply because of
the amount of people. It's also a mentality thing. Europeans simply want
to always win and be the best; moreso than the average American. To get
back to V:TES. So you go to some 30 player tournament with a "creative,
but working" deck. You hope to get into the finals and maybe even talk
your way into a win. Of course, may other people will do the same and
some will just play whatever is strong.

The average European will ALWAYS play to win in a game that's of any
importance. No inventive stuff, no creative decks (those only get played
in friendly games), just the best decks around. Of course you'll see an
odd fun theme deck around once in a while, but we're talking the middle
of the road player here. A good 75% of the participants will play decks
that are condidered strong; few moving parts, low average cap, not combo
dependant. I was merely suggesting the possibility that this mentality,
or, if you wish, emotional involvement reduces the strength of PtO.

There must be SOME explanation why most Europeans here couldn't care
less about PtO and most Americans hate it with a passion.

> > I'm glad some actual European chimed in with a sweeping
> > generalization. I was expected to get called a nazi by at least one

Your "statistical" analysis is flawed. The main flaw in your logic at
this point is that the culture in the US and the culture in Europe place
different values on different sports. So, to expect the US to compete as
"statistically" as they should in soccer as landmass, population, and other
factors would indicate is folly, because the culture here in the US does not
place as much value in soccer as Europe does. I daresay that if soccer were
the main sport in the US and in Europe that the numbers would come close to
to matching what you seem to think is expected.
Of course my assumption has no basis, however, it is relatively safe to
assume that if a lot of the capable athletes were to have received soccer
training instead of say...baseball training, or American football training,
or basketball training, they would probably play soccer pretty well. Yes
these sports require different sorts of physical activity and I'm sure not
all athletes in these sports would do well, however, their innate physical
talent is great enough that I am willing to say they could probably have
played soccer very well had they received the proper impetus in their
younger years. Keep in mind that these are not normal people like you (I'm
assuming you're not a pro-sports player) but that these are people with
distinct physical gifts, gifts that must be properly channeled and could be
channeled in many directions.
So before you go around saying the US doesn't want to "be the best," try
to consider other possibilities that could explain what's going on.

> The average European will ALWAYS play to win in a game that's of any
> importance. No inventive stuff, no creative decks (those only get played
> in friendly games), just the best decks around. Of course you'll see an
> odd fun theme deck around once in a while, but we're talking the middle
> of the road player here. A good 75% of the participants will play decks
> that are condidered strong; few moving parts, low average cap, not combo
> dependant. I was merely suggesting the possibility that this mentality,
> or, if you wish, emotional involvement reduces the strength of PtO.
>
> There must be SOME explanation why most Europeans here couldn't care
> less about PtO and most Americans hate it with a passion.

There is nothing that makes an inventive or creative deck any weaker
than traditional decks. You seem to equate creative with weak, which simply
is not the case. Do creative decks win in unconventional ways? Sometimes.
Do creative decks win in unexpected ways? Most of the time. Just because a
deck takes an alternate path to victory does not make it any weaker than any
deck that's been proven to work. In fact, it could help you win if nobody's
ever seen a deck like it before, because your opponents probably haven't
accounted for it in their list of defenses and thus are less prepared to
handle it. But to imply that people in the US aren't attempting to play to
win and just want to play for creativity's sake is again, folly.

No, but I play against Europeans all the time on deckbot. You should come

It's a great influence in both my local metagame, in my choices for
tournament play, and in my play on deckbot against a world-wide pool of

problem, and most of the players of such decks *have* been European, FWIW.

Mmm... In fact it's not so easy : I like to play votes (especially sabbat
voters ) and i can recall two or three finals ruined by the extensive use of
delaying tactics by my prey or predator, and even grand predator. Couldn't
get to pass 5 votes in a row and it coste me the game =)

most votes require a little setting and a good timing to be called.
Calling a parity shift (or Transfer of power -yeah i play this shit) , and
being delayed does not guarantee you that your prey, predator or other
possible target will have the same amount of pool on the following turn. You
can't guarantee that they will have the same number of minions tapped for a
domain challenge, the same amount of blood on their vamps for a free states
rant. Plus , often, the player laying a delaying tactics will wait to the
point you have spend cards like Telepathic vote counting, bewitching
oration, tapped your demonstration etc... So you just lost precious cards
and missed the oportunity to voter cap (if any). Some very useful votes in
heavy voter decks like reins of power, political stranglehold can't be
called again so your machiavelic plans all go to the trashbin with a single
card.
But the worst effect when a delaying tactics is played is that you lost all
surprise factor and you don't ever know if your vampires will stand here
next turn or be turned to ashes by the nearby fighter.
Example : Marcus vitel calls a Banishment on my predator's Jalan Ajav. If
the vote is delayed -and it can happen either by your prey ("let jalan put
pressure on my predator!) your predator ("i won't let you banish my
minions") or even your grand prey ("if jalan is still ready next turn, he
will rush and torporize marcus vittel, guranteed"), the you can say bye bye
to your voters because the punching machine will come directly to you.
Not to count table split deals like "let me kill the damn voting bastard and
i'll roll over")

I think it's especially true for a strong vote like protect thine own. If
the IC lightning hamer mises the target (most often due to DT), the IC is in
deep trouble.

It's because i endured the troubles facing delaying tactics, that now i pack
at least three in all my decks. And also because sitching places to steal
VP's is plain bad. Yeah sorry for all those people who did the job for me :
i know it's bad but it's so much fun, the loook on your face when i simply
take the ripe fruits from the tree you've just shaken =)

Politics in jyhad are difficult to handle but allow you to do very unique
things : switching places, making people pay for playing their turns, steal
pool from other players -and even burn other vampires right away.
I just think the best answer to all of this is Delaying tactics. Pack some
more and you'll see that life is better when you don't get your vp stolen or
your vampires burnt =)

reyda

Messages.Author: Azel
Messages.Body:
y'see... blocking PTO isn't really the *big thing* we who don't like it
focus on. For the sake of argument, sure PTO is "equally blockable." Even
though it does have an inherent +1 stealth, has an alternate use of burning
for +1 vote, and can target directly a vampire even though it's an
undirected action (for table crossing). but barring all that - and the
majority of ICs having general access to "block fails" cards - the
referrendum is no where near an unpredictable place like combat.

The means of defense are poor, and already the referrendum starts with 5
votes for. I don't know how your playgroup works, but even seasoned players
here admit that unless you are a devoted vote player yourself the casual
vote defense cards just don't cut it like the casual combat defense
available out there. It is hardly that hard to vote lock, especially with an
IC vote deck. So the struggles in the referrendum are just staving off the
inevitable, unless you have some reliable permanent table votes. Now
plopping PTO into the mix, in an environment of the game mechanic that isn't
that hard to overwhelm, that takes an effect beyond the scope of even the
most galling combat cards is just wrong.

Yes, yes, I hear about Amaranth, and Coma and Entombment et al. But
seriously, read the text again. Combat - you have to get into combat,
preferrably with a particular minion, which therefore generally necessitates
another card. And Amaranth exposes you to diablerie's drawback of the blood
hunt, something PTO does not. Coma and Entombment only send you to torpor,
for a hefty blood cost unusual to most combat cards. And these are but mere
strike cards, in a game mechanic environment that is notoriously diverse and
filled with strong countermeasures. PTO? final death, do not pass go, do not
collect $200. that's it, nothing. no penalty. from a simple action at +1
that has low opportunity cost.

and this nowhere deals with big votes routine ability to bloat in obscene
proportions, therefore ignoring most of your bleed damage. nor does it deal
with casual anti-defense so strong as to ignore the majority of your
rushing. y'know, i believe that is fair and all for playing a big vamp - big
bloating and teflon coating - but to add a vote action that blithely piffs
away a minion without significant recourse or significant opportunity cost
is just sheer poor design.

the opportunity cost before was the non-camarilla vampires were a
significant minority in the game. now that opportunity cost is undeniably no
longer there.

the other opportunity cost of playing an IC member and using vote cards?
Laughable. Sure playing with big vampires is an opportunity cost in an of
itself, but are you saying we are such inept deck designers that we don't
know how to get around such a problem? Undoubtedly you've seen those playing
large cap vampires, they were obviously able to work around that. And with
vote you can work around it with great success to the point of even bloating
back pool. So obviously people worked around this precious argument, and to
an incredible degree of success, and therefore has eternally nulled this
line of reasoning. It is the unfairness of having a cardre of large caps
being able to abuse an unfair and unbelievably simple combo that is being
argued.

generally one card that was poorly thought about, or worked so well with
current conditions or previous cards that warranted it to be restricted or
banned. it wasn't hard to see in that game if a combo was egregiously
overpowered, because in a duel you can isolate the swing effects of a single
card. but vtes it's a bit harder due to multiplayer reasons. but even so we
can see there is still such egregious swings of power by a simplistic combo
that doesn't strain the decks construction in any significant manner. if a
combo only necessitates a splash of 2-4 copies of the same card in an
already existing strategy to have drastic play dynamic effects then
obviously there's something wrong. at least when i ask players of other CCG
that same question they say that. and i happen to agree.

then can fight quite effectively though not as well as a well played

intercept deck should be able to defend himself withoutt specifric

fighter as Thetmes, then the problem is not Protect Thine Own.

comes out.

fact that Justicar's retribution is espiaclly powerfull in these

that and

Nowhere in the game can you define this second is the necessary,
automatic, direct consequence of the first situation.

you're saying.

deck-end playstyles is big enough, you might actually see it.

limitations of gatheringt this info on an NG..

untill that time, I believe what I believe, you believe what you
believe.We're probably into such different gaming environments, with
such a different view, that we'll never actually convince each other.

greetz

Messages.Author: Curevei
Messages.Body:
>Who really cares about PTO? It is a sloppy design but there are bigger
>fish to fry.

Okay, I think there are bigger fish to fry then PTO. I've contributed to the
endless PTO debate not because I think it's the most important change the game
needs but because it could, in theory, fry quickly.

So, what is the most pressing fix the game needs? Or, since there's going to
be a lot of disagreement, what are the most pressing fixes without going
overboard?

There are a lot of cards I don't like in the game, but even as dumb as I think
some cards are, I don't rate errataing or banning a particular card the top
priority nor do I think it's most essential to create new cards that make old,
library cards significantly better as to make them worth playing. There are
certain fundamental features of the game that bug me even if they aren't
entirely bad. One being the limited paths to victory, though this has the
benefit of keeping the game under control, of providing a solid framework for
having a multiplayer CCG work well mechanically even if it contributes to it
becoming stale over time. Another, older complaint being the extremeness in
the details - combats being too much carnage or too little, bleeds being too
big, etc.

While it's not *obviously* the most bothersome issue and, for all I know, it's
just the bitch of the year or has been highlighted due to the storyline events,
I think the thing about the game that bothers me the most is how little what's
really good changes. For all that players handle Dom/Obf better now than they
once did, whether due to being better players or because the card pool has
changed, it's still studly. Just consider if there weren't so many crap Jyhad
vampires and the group 1 Malks had some depth to their worth playing vampires.
Aus/Dem/Obf. Dom + stealth. P/J. Weenie. Etc.

The game has evolved. Evolved even towards a more balanced environment. But,
it's slow and it's incomplete (okay, incomplete is a bad word with evolution -
insufficient). It's good that clans that suck and disciplines that suck get
help to make them somewhat better, but to keep the game lively, what should be
best should be changing as well. It's not that I care whether the Assamites
are the best clan in the game for 6 months, but I do care that some currently
lesser clans get their moment in the sun, so to speak. And, really, over the
course of the game, every clan should have an opportunity at the top, every
discipline should be the Dominate of the game for a while, every bundle of
titles should be abbreviated in tournament winning decks as P/J are, and so
forth.

That's not the point at all. The point is that "my" trick (and it's not
"mine", as much as the "pro Protect Thine Own" players may feel like the
"anti PTO players" love combat and hate vote, I am perfectly willing and
able to play with PTO myself as long as it remains an unfair card, and I
don't play that much combat these days - sorry for the tangent) is

The PTO "trick", on the other hand, requires at least one card (an
intercept or a Direct Intervention) to foil and can un-foil itself by
using one of the other cards that are likely to be in its own library
(just because they're generally useful cards, not specifically because
it needs them to be able to play PTO).

Sure, no combat defense is absolute either, but (a) burning vampires in
combat is *a lot* harder than burning them with PTO, as it *always*
requires more than one card, and (b) burning vampires in combat is
generally blockable at 0 intercept, ie by the smallest vampire you have
(since stealth-rush isn't all that likely, as stealth's synergy with
rush isn't very strong), whereas blocking a PTO requires at least 1
intercept and may often require more (since stealth-vote is a great plan
that wins games, in my experience).

> If your Laz blocks the PtO (which he may have a huge chane to do,
> especially considering the possibility of a DI on Elder
> Impersonnation) then I suggest the IC is dead.

Do you hear what you're saying? The possibility of a DI on Elder
Impersonation? That means paying a pool to be able to block what has
otherwise become unblockable to you, and having one specific card in
hand at the right moment. It also means that you had enough intercept
for the Inner Circle member to have felt the need to play the Elder
Impersonation, and you have now wasted that intercept unless you *do*
have the DI in hand. If you had the DI, you'd be a *lot* safer playing
it on the Protect Thine Own itself - in which case the PTO player got to
"bleed you for 1" and use up your master phase action (and ability to DI
again before your next turn!) while remaining untapped to do something
else.

> combat vs a combat monster like Lazve is almost certain death for non

That's simply not true. Any IC member with Dominate can play Obedience
against Lazverinus... or any other vampire that's likely to be rushing
it. Many of them have the possibility of going to long range and using
a Combat Ends, as well.

> So a good
> intercept deck should be able to defend himself withoutt specifric
> cards ( and NO, eagle sight is not a specific card)

Uh... how exactly is Eagle's Sight not a specific card? Are there lots
of cards that do the same thing as Eagle's Sight? Do they exist for
several common disciplines, so that you can use them even if you don't
have superior Auspex?

Perhaps what you're trying to say here is that a "good intercept deck"
must use superior Auspex and must include Eagle's Sight anyway, just as
a prerequisite for being a good intercept deck. Perhaps that's true.
But it doesn't give any consolation to people who might want to play
something *other* than a "good intercept deck".

> If you play rush with your thetmes, I suggest you rush the IC before.

> If the problem is that you cannot rush the IC while playing such a big
> fighter as Thetmes, then the problem is not Protect Thine Own.

No... the problem *is* Protect Thine Own. It's the PTO that lets the IC
member strike preemptively against any non-Camarilla vampire it chooses,
for the cost of one card, one blood, and one political action. Would it
be OK for this card to exist?

"Protect Thy Turf
Action
1 stealth
1 blood
Requires a non-Camarilla vampire of at least 8 capacity with 3 votes, or
a non-Camarilla vampire of 11 capacity. Choose a Camarilla vampire with
capacity below 6, or if the acting vampire has 11 capacity, choose any
Camarilla vampire. That vampire is burned."

I know it's not an exact comparison because this action is not a vote -
that seems fair because the non-Camarilla don't have any 4-vote +2 bleed
vampires to play it with. It's still a pretty close comparison - it's
even a lot weaker on the targeting section because (a) there are fewer
Camarilla vampires in print than there are non-Cam, and (b) there are
only 4 vampires in print who can play this "out of the box" to burn any
Cam vampire.

But if you don't think this card would be fair, how can Protect Thine
Own be fair?

Burning a ready vampire with no restriction on capacity as a 1 stealth
action is simply too large an effect for any single card to have -
whether it's a vote or not. It's Just Not A Fair Effect. It doesn't
matter if it's "possible" to counter it by making your opponent unable
to play it before they actually get to play it, or if it can be stopped
with Direct Intervention (the "DI defense", by the way, is not exactly
plausible in that it existed *just as much* for the only cards in the
game that some people have been willing to admit *ever* needed fixing -
Monocle of Clarity and The Return to Innocence). A single card *should
not have such a large effect*. It's *not appropriate to the game of
VTES*.

And that's nearly all that can be said about it. If you don't believe
that there even *can* be such a thing as an effect that's too great for
a single card to have, I guess you'll never see what I (and others) have
been trying to get at.

Josh

rotation
> (rotating out the old "good" cards).
>
> Which are you proposing (or is there something else you had in mind)?

Power escalation is a problem if you escalate power relative to "the
best cards in the game." It's probably *not* a problem if you escalate
power relative to "the cards that currently exist for discipline X", if
those cards are currently weak relative to the best cards in the game.

That is, it seems like it would not be bad for the game as a whole if
Quietus were to start getting cards as powerful as Govern the Unaligned
and Deflection. They would be escalated hugely in power over things
like Foul Blood, sure, but as long as you don't escalate power above the
strongest cards in the game - which we already accept that people can
and will play - I don't think it should give the game an "escalation
problem".

Set rotation has a certain appeal too, but obviously tends to piss off
the existing player base. Unlike Magic, I suspect that we don't have a
big enough (or easily-expandable-enough) player base to be able to shrug
that off. :-)

Of course, I'm always interested in third-solution ideas too...

Josh

>The ways to accomplish that are by power escalation or by card set rotation
>(rotating out the old "good" cards).
>
>Which are you proposing (or is there something else you had in mind)?

My first thought is what Josh said about escalating power in parts of the game
to match other parts. It's likely to have some sort of overall power
escalation effect, but it's possible that it can be kept under control.

Isn't this, to an extent, what's being done already? For instance, Deed the
Heart's Desire sets up making Quietus a vastly better discipline once Quietus
or Assamites (since they have Quietus) get worthwhile actions to go with it.
Is the plan to never give them those actions?

Or, if you don't like conjecture, isn't this what happened to some extent with
independents (besides Assamites) and Final Nights? The difference being,
instead of elevating the independents to decent status, they could have been
elevated to first tier status. Now, at some point, to get evolution at the
top, what was once mighty and not so anymore would have to be elevated again
somehow, which ultimately means power escalation.

Power escalation can easily get out of hand, but zero escalation is a stale
game. I'm not, therefore, against power escalation per se. If the game takes
3 years to see dramatic power escalation, um, okay, I don't see the big deal.

Nor am I against rotation. The reality of CCGs is that they become
increasingly cumbersome unless something is done to reboot the environment
either by a game reboot or by rotation.

I realize that there's likely an enormous resistance to creating a true "type
2" environment even if CCGs besides Magic have gone that path. Already, one
hears comments from existing players how they would be happy if the game
stopped expanding. That might indeed produce the optimal game as many a CCG
has gotten declined from some peak that seems to center around the two
expansion period. Maybe it's possible that a static CCG is worth playing in
perpetuity. But, it artificially limits the game, much like putting out weak
cards and new strategies that are weak.

That might not be too clear in meaning. This may not help, but here's a go
anyway. For people who don't need anything new to maintain interest, they have
the choice of not using anything new, less than ideal choice but it exists.
Adding nothing new that's interesting removes the choice from people who want
something new to play with that which interests them.

There is the possibility, though it's exceedingly hard to manage, that
increases in strategic variety can change the balance of power without
overblown power escalation. I think this is what you've been trying to do.
The problem is that, if only because there was so little balance to begin with,
that the shifts in balance of power have been too small. Any CCG needs a
shaking up to some degree regularly, if not often.

As I just said to somebody, I can survive on new style without new substance,
e.g. new clans and new disciplines that really don't do anything significant
new or different besides being new and supposedly different. This path, I'm
sure, would satisfy a lot of other people as well given how warmly Bloodlines
has been embraced.

There was a time, back when Sabbat was easy to get, that I wanted to play in a
Sabbat only environment. Not all of the time, of course, but regularly. While
it may not have been a great environment (I don't know), there were differences
in the balance of power (obviously) that I thought would make the game feel
fresher. Now, it's entirely possible to do that now. The problem being
getting people to cooperate. There's no encouragement for such alternate
environments outside of the relatively minor differences in storyline as
there's a lack of sanctioning, whether real or perceived, for doing something
different with the game. If the game, with its standard card pool, does it
"naturally" through expansion, then the need is no longer there to try to
create it artificially, to get people's cooperation, something which they
aren't likely to give.

> For good players goes this: I have never met really good top level
> payers that can, from the bottom of their heart 100* honestly claim

Hopefully I'm not putting words in other people's mouths with this, but I
believe the following people have publicly stated that PTO is
broken/unfair/too good:

Josh Duffin
Jeff Thompson
Derek Ray
Peter Bakija
Snapcase
Jeff Kuta

My apologies for the others that I know I've overlooked, but those are
some people who have participated heavily in the discussions here, have
all won tournaments, and all of whom I regard as excellent players. You
just told them they sucked.

I think it would be much, *much* more productive to leave out any
considerations of how good a player might be, or what their metagame might
be like, and just stick to the game mechanics. Yes, Paris has an enormous
number of players but, for god's sake, there are good players elsewhere.

> The ball: It is not *so* much riskier for large non-cam's. It is 1
> card which a reqiurement of IC we're talking about.
> How many times have you come prepared for PTO (even when playing large
> non-cammies) and got beaten by it?

This side-steps the issue of whether incorporating vote defense is
feasible. It boils down to DI, a poor argument for anything, and DT. I
assume you've read all the discussion about DT that's already occurred.
If you didn't find any of the explanations of its inadequacy compelling
before, I don't see that repeating them will have much of an effect.

I myself have argued in the past the importance of timing in the game.
Most recently, in the context of extracting pool via succubus club in
return for not rushing. There is a distinction between never being rushed
at all, which is a silly premise to build a deal upon, and not being
rushed *right now*. So, I think I have some grasp of the delicacies of
timing. That said, I believe the ability to stave off the effect of PTO
for a turn is the best defense out there, but ultimately a poor
counter-argument to the proposition that the effect is too large,
inappropriate, or whatever language you choose for "me no likey".

> My point is: you *don't* have to fall back to DI.It's one (and an
> obvious and simple ) solution to the PTO problem.

But if DI is the *only* answer to the problem, then *that* is a problem in
itself, correct? I understand that you disagree about the efficacy of DT,
but I think we will have to just agree to disagree on that, as I have
nothing new to say on it. The third option, choosing a deck that isn't
vulnerable to PTO either because of sect composition or average capacity,
is begging the question. It seems to me that, in this light, PTO remains
a problem.

> As everything can be DI-ed, indeed, its solves the problem as any
> other solution, right?DI came up nt as the sole defense, it came up in
> the list of defenses against PTO...

>> > No they wont. Not necessarily.Whenever I play tournaments, I always
>> > include DT and DI's.You can always ask Reyda to testify what the
>> > effects of that are on political decks being payed at those tables.

I'm familiar with the effects of the cards, having played it and seen it
played for years. It is also possible that you choose decks that are
strong enough in their basic strategy, e.g. mid-cap stealth bleed that
also gains pool via its bleed mechanic (just as an example) that it has
plenty of room left over for such extras. That is a good deck. There
should be more good decks possible, and not every deck is going to have
the luxury of playing stealth bleed with midcaps (for example).

The core of this argument is that the *possibility* of PTO is sufficient
to deter playing 8 - 11 cap non-cams in tournaments. This idea is
predicated upon the premise that there is no adequate defense against this
card, most especially if you are targeted from across the table by it. If
you are fine with the idea that such vampires have no place within a
tournament game anyway, then you of course are not going to see it as a
problem. Personally, I think that is a ridiculous position to take.

> You find it does more than 1 card should do.
> I simply fail to grasp, as not a single anti PTO person seem to be
> able to: why???

I'm not sure I'm parsing your sentence as you intend, as I would ask
"what" not a single anti-PTO person is able to.... do? say? grasp? But
if you are asking for explanations as to why the card is overpowered, I
can only refer you to the previous 250+ threads. I have nothing new to
add on that front.

> Getting your vampires burned happens in all kinds of ways AS WELL, and
> in some games more than pool loss BTW...everybody has to account for
> it.

The other ways in which vampires are burned are: A) equally applicable to
vampires of all sects, and B) require much more set up, and C) much easier
to defend against. This goes against my decision to avoid repeating
myself and others, but I saw an opportunity to do so succinctly.

> Please define "Tactical Nuke Magnitude" in a way so we can discuss it.

Choose a vampire. Burn it. That would be "tactical nuke" magnitude.

> Do you think putting Succubus Club in play is of tactical magnitude?

Not really the same thing, but the way in which it facilitates spiteful
losing is a sufficient reason in my mind for banning it, if that's what
you are getting at.

> Do
> you think getting another turn is?

No, and I see the obvious followup to this, if you care to save yourself,
and then myself, some typing.

> I don't fel inclined to call PTO in
> any way orbital by the way..

The "orbital" bit alludes to the fact that you can be targeted by it with
no chance to block it, barring eagle's sight. Less strongly, it also
alludes to its inherent stealth, and the relative strengths of stealth vs.
intercept.

> There are. They are the same defenses as the ones you should be
> including against*any* political deck.And that's not too hard these
> days.

Uh, yes it is. If you know of some defenses besides DI, DT, and Vox,
please let me know. And there is no vote that has so immediate an impact
on your game as this card. Note that there have not been repeated
arguments that "politics is broken". The problem is with the effects of
this card, not vast swaths of players low-balling their politics defense
in the hopes of not getting nailed by it.

Also, as an aside, the best politics defense is to have titled vampires in
play, not some reaction card or OOT master. Sadly, most of these table
votes will manifest in the form of P/J titles, who will not care about PTO
and further may conspire with you to benefit from it's passing.

> No necessarily.I'm starting to belive you've seldom seen a well-played
> PS now.

And I am starting to believe you are yet another snotty little person who
just can't *quite* bring himself to leave the ad hominem at home. Or do
you think "play PS on key blocker, swarm in with my wave of Sooper Sekrit
Stealth Bleed, oust" is some special Parisian technique? Design something
original, then get an attitude.

> Read the whole list of "things you an do against/about PTO".People seem
> to insist on PTO being broken cause it can burn high cap non cammies. It
> is simply not a guaranteed way of doing that.Taking out a cornerstone
> vamp is simply not a guarantueed oust.

Read it? Hell, I *wrote* a good chunk of it. I started the thing over on
Path of Blood, and Jeff Kuta brought it here. I suggest reading it
yourself, as everything you touch upon has been raised and answered,
exhaustively.

> Again, if "being a legal target for PTO or not" is the first and/or only
> thing people take into account when deciding which vamps to play, I'm
> not surprised to find they get ousted very often. Such a way of thinking
> would IMO represent a complete screwed up/silly/illogical/ childish view
> of the game.

Who said it is first or only? It is *a* consideration, and a serious one.
Your further ad hominem is built upon a straw man. Man, you are willing
to work hard for you ad hominems, aren't you?

> How often do you play single sect decks?

Quite often, usually due to playing disciplines that only occur within a
single clan.

>or strictly indies?or strictly
> indies/non-cammies?

Again, a lot. Is that bad? If so much diversity exists in the card game,
shouldn't at least a majority of it stand on equal footing to the three or
four decks that *most of us* identify within a few months of learning the
game? If so, how will one know without playing them at the highest level?

David Cherryholmes

Messages.Author: Aramis
Messages.Body:
I find myself nodding when I read Josh's post. Although I think the
larger theme I want to see is every clan having an area within which
they are on par with the long-established top clans of the game. Not
every group should be good at everything, but each group needs
something to make you want to play with them. The problem I think we
see currently is that while each clan/discipline has a unique
"flavor", they are not all equally good at winning the game. So
people who play those groups of vampires usually either end up playing
handicapped with less powerful options, or grafting out-of-clan
elements onto their deck design (Gangrel w/Dominate come to mind).

I thought the best design decision to date was the creation of
dual-discipline cards. They allow powerful effects to be designed and
targeted to help balance out the weaker clans without giving further
advantage to the established groups. Although, just giving the
underpowered disciplines (quietus, etc.) good cards to start with
would probably be a more direct fix.

If the player base doesn't like expansions and WW doesn't care about making
money off of the game, then isn't the answer to stop expanding? I don't think
either is true. In fact, I think both must be false. Players must want
expansions or they wouldn't sell, for instance. If players want expansions,
then it follows that they don't want the game to be stagnant. If they don't
want the game to be stagnant, then some power escalation must occur simply
because the only way true stagnation can happen when new cards come out is that
no one plays the new cards, at least on a tournament level.

Once you buy into some power escalation, then it's a matter of degree, and the
degree I'm looking for is one that I think it perfectly reasonable - what's
best evolves over time.

>> But, it artificially limits the game, much like putting out weak
>> cards and new strategies that are weak.
>
>A design decision not to introduce power escalation is a limit of sorts, yes.
>The question is whether it's a good limit to have.

I've noticed a pattern with CCGs. Some expansion comes out that has minor
impact on the competitive level of the game. Afterwards, expansions come out
that are much more powerful. Could be cynical and say that the reason this
occurs is that the company wants to make more money and powerful sets
necessitate people buying cards to remain competitive where weak sets don't.
Does it matter ... when people buy them?

What I haven't noticed is a pattern where the putting out of powerful sets has
killed a CCG. Now, it seems exceedingly difficult to figure out the precise
causes and the proportions they contribute to why a CCG dies, but my experience
with one company has been that they often wrongly attributed the causes for why
something like poor sales of a set have occurred. Anyway, point being that
power escalation may make a game less optimized, but it may also keep games
alive.

>> That might not be too clear in meaning. This may not help, but here's a go
>> anyway. For people who don't need anything new to maintain interest, they
>have
>> the choice of not using anything new, less than ideal choice but it exists.
>
>> Adding nothing new that's interesting removes the choice from people who
>want
>> something new to play with that which interests them.
>
>> There is the possibility, though it's exceedingly hard to manage, that
>> increases in strategic variety can change the balance of power without
>> overblown power escalation. I think this is what you've been trying to do.
>
>
>Right.
>See Black Hand for example. Power Escalation isn't a necessary condition for
>interesting.

I find the stuff in BH that's interesting is the stuff that can have impact on
a competitive level. While loads better than Anarchs, I still see a bunch of
junk/filler in BH that drags the set down.

Bloodlines would be a much better example. This is why I push for more clans
and more disciplines - it's easier to disguise weakness in something completely
novel than it is to disguise weakness in something already figured out.
Fortunately, it takes years for V:TES players to figure out new cards where it
only takes a couple of months for players of other CCGs. (If you think this is
a swipe, see comments to as much posted here not too infrequently.)

>> The problem is that, if only because there was so little balance to begin
>with,
>> that the shifts in balance of power have been too small. Any CCG needs a
>> shaking up to some degree regularly, if not often.
>
>You need an "IMO" at the end there, IMO. More fodder for the polls, at any
>rate.

Do you actually care about the polls? I'm not sure why. Only a fraction of
the player base is even aware they exist. Only another fraction will vote.
The people who do vote may care more on the issue, which is good for the
validity of the poll, but they also tend to be people who care more about
saying something, anything regardless as to subject or interest, which is bad
for the validity of the poll. Then, the questions are often poorly
constructed. The options given too often have biases towards certain answers.

Couldn't you (someone in WW) do a sampling of a decent number of known players?
This retains certain biases, like that known players is only some fraction of
the player base, but it should be a more balanced view.

Personally, if I were running the show, I'd try to analyze sales numbers as
they would at least cover the entirety of the customer base. Though, I could
see pain in trying to figure out what's what through them as factors such as
the economy in general, the CCG economy, timing of sets, and whatever else
could affect numbers. And, BTW, rather than make the mistake Precedence did by
believing that poor sales for a set indicated disdain for that set, I would try
to gauge the hangover effect that a poorly taken set has on the next set.

>would probably be a more direct fix.

All of these pent up rants.

Vicissitude, Obtenebration, Dementation. These are really good disciplines.
Add one inclan discipline to them, and they are "whole".

Chimerstry, Necromancy, Quietus, Serpentis. Chimerstry is really good if you
don't pay full cost for it. Necromancy is okay, having some nice cards, a

Quietus blows.

So, what's the point? The point is that certain clans in the game have their
own discipline (going to ignore bloodlines for the moment). Those with a
strong, unique discipline are far stronger than those without. While not
difficult to run into problems pumping a weak, common discipline like Celerity
as you may can make clans like (!)Toreador even better, pumping a not strong,

controllable.

Messages.Body:
"LSJ" <vte...@white-wolf.com> wrote in message
news:3FFEA731...@white-wolf.com...
> Curevei wrote:

> > Isn't this, to an extent, what's being done already? For instance,
Deed the

once Quietus

with it.

>

>

> But your original message indicated that you wanted cards introduced
to make, say,
> Quietus *exceed* Dominate (to be "at the top"). And then add some
cards to another
> Discipline to it exceed Quietus (to be "at the top for a while"). And
so on.
>
> Which, as near as I can figure, involves strict escalation unless card
rotation
> is involved.

To me, Quietus doesn't have to exceed Dominate (or Presence, or
Obfuscate). It just ought to *equal* it. I haven't really seen
sufficient evidence in terms of cards printed to show that this
(equalizing power of disciplines) has been a design goal, unless it's
supposed to take 15 years for the goal to be reached. (I don't mean
that as a slam, but there does seem to me to be a great reluctance to
ever create anything new that rivals the power of Govern the Unaligned
or Deflection. And while I sympathize with that reluctance, as you can
see from my Jyhad "done right" idea, in a world where Govern and
Deflection are always going to exist, I think it is the right thing to
do to make other cards that are as good for the disciplines and clans
that have historically been weaker.)

> > Is the plan to never give them those actions?
>
> ?
> Of course not, if by worthwhile you mean balanced.

Is Govern the Unaligned a "balanced" action? If it is, things on that
level would be plenty worthwhile for the Assamites to get. But if it's
not, then the Assamites (or Quietus, or whatever) might need to get some
"unbalanced" actions to truly compete with the strong clans.

> > Power escalation can easily get out of hand, but zero escalation is
a stale
> > game. I'm not, therefore, against power escalation per se. If the
game takes
> > 3 years to see dramatic power escalation, um, okay, I don't see the
big deal.
>
> That might make good fodder for a pool for someone.

I wouldn't have thought you would trust polls (assuming you do mean
polls and not pools in the "betting pool" sense, which is what I thought
at first) as an accurate means of even gauging player-base opinion, let
alone for determining the proper direction for the game. I'm sure you
know that amateur polls of the kind we can actually do aren't very
scientific and are therefore not necessarily very accurate at all.

That said, if White Wolf can hire a polling firm to do some good surveys
of VTES players, I would be absolutely thrilled to see some results on
VTES topics.

> > Nor am I against rotation. The reality of CCGs is that they become
> > increasingly cumbersome unless something is done to reboot the
environment
> > either by a game reboot or by rotation.
>
> That might make more good fodder.
> Note the reaction to the grouping rule - a pale shadow of actual
rotation.

Yes, exactly. Rotation pisses people off. And we might not have the
playerbase to support it. But it was done in Magic for a reason... and
it lets them introduce new cards that are tournament-worthy without
straight-up power escalation.

The only real alternative is to eventually (who knows how long
eventually is, it certainly varies by the game and the players involved)
let the game die, or become stagnant, or accept escalation. Unless,
again, you know of another way.

> > Maybe it's possible that a static CCG is worth playing in
> > perpetuity.
>
> It sure seemed that it was possible back in 1999.

?
I don't think 3 years equals perpetuity.

And I don't think all the VTES players who were into the game in 1994,
1995, 1996 were still into it in 1999, either. And I don't think there
were as many playing in 1999 as were playing in 2001 or 2002 or 2003.

A static CCG may well be worth playing to *some* people in perpetuity,
but I really believe that that's going to be a *much* smaller audience -
and a shrinking one - compared to the people it can attract with ongoing
meaniningful expansion.

> > But, it artificially limits the game, much like putting out weak
> > cards and new strategies that are weak.
>
> A design decision not to introduce power escalation is a limit of
sorts, yes.
> The question is whether it's a good limit to have.

I don't think you should blithely assume that it *is* a good limit to
have. I'm somewhat familiar with two other relatively-lively CCGs:
Magic and Shadowfist. Both have seen their share of power escalation
(at least in some sense) over the years. I think that stringently
avoiding *any* power escalation is likely to become a handicap at least
as harmful to the game as allowing "some" power escalation would be.
(Even VTES has seen "some", in the vampire design criteria. Not
necessarily under your watch, initially, of course.)

> > There is the possibility, though it's exceedingly hard to manage,
that
> > increases in strategic variety can change the balance of power
without
> > overblown power escalation. I think this is what you've been trying
to do.
>
> Right.
> See Black Hand for example. Power Escalation isn't a necessary
condition for
> interesting.

But it's so hard - it really is, and you've probably noticed it yourself
in card design - to make very many "interesting" cards (ie not only
increasing variety but strong enough to successfully compete for card
slots in tournament decks) *without* letting them escalate power - at
least within their "niche", if their niche is one that has in the past
had relatively weak cards or effects.

I think I would take it farther than Ian and say that the increases in
strategic variety we've actually seen in the past few expansions
*haven't* significantly changed the balance of power, except perhaps in
weakening weenie decks somewhat. (Stealth-bleed and vote decks have
been nearly unaffected.) As Ian wrote below, the shifts in power may
exist, but they're not big enough relative to the preexisting
*im*balances in power.

> > The problem is that, if only because there was so little balance to
begin with,
> > that the shifts in balance of power have been too small. Any CCG
needs a
> > shaking up to some degree regularly, if not often.
>
> You need an "IMO" at the end there, IMO. More fodder for the polls, at
any rate.

Much like editorial-page pieces in the newspaper, newsgroup posts don't
normally need "IMOs" in that everything in them is naturally the opinion
of the writer, unless there are statistical analyses involved or
something. Actually putting the "IMO" in is kind of like using
smilies - it emphasizes that this is an especially opinion-based
sentence, or something. Well, IMO, anyway. :-)

Anyhow, if you dispute that every CCG needs shaking up occasionally,
isn't the alternative to claim that the CCG would be fine without ever
changing in any real way? Which is a claim that you could make, but it
would suggest never bothering to print expansions at all rather than
going to the effort (and it's a lot of effort) without wanting to allow
the new cards to really change the game.

I'm not unreservedly in favor of power escalation. But at least to the
point of making the weak clans and disciplines *as* strong as the
existing strong clans/disciplines, I don't think it should be
preemptively written off, either.

Josh

and into the fire

Messages.Body:
> Vicissitude, Obtenebration, Dementation. These are really good disciplines.
> Add one inclan discipline to them, and they are "whole".

Vic and Obt are both very strong support disciplines. Dementation is
what Dominate should be -- strong bleed, but more support actions and
less sheer power -- and no bounce.

> Chimerstry, Necromancy, Quietus, Serpentis. Chimerstry is really good if you
> don't pay full cost for it.

Some of the effects are still strong if you pay full cost, though it
is the most expensive discipline in the game. Sensory Dep is worth
three blood if you can keep your vampires alive. Reality works well
with Trick of the Danyaa. It works well by itself, and it synergizes
perfectly with Fortitude and Animalism. Thanks to Draba, the Ravnos
are the strongest defensive clan in the game, IMO, which they pay for
in reduced in-clan ousting power.

>Necromancy is okay, having some nice cards, a little depth.

It is a solid support discipline. Not Obtenebration-strength, but
it's a good replacement for Obfuscate (and in intercept-heavy
environments, better).

>Serpentis has a very small number of strong cards and no depth.

Too focused on a difficult strategy. They could use some versatility.

> Quietus blows.

Outside of combat, yes. In combat, it's very strong. Burn blood,
unpreventable damage, aggravated damage. The only things it misses
are anti S:CE and maneuvers, which are supplied by the other two
Assamite inclans in abundance. It synergizes very well -- but it is
probably the worst at standing alone.

> Or, maybe the point is one wonders why the independents' disciplines haven't
> gotten a greater boost already.

The last time the four original independents got a set focus, they got
a huge boost. Mostly.

Assamites became as deadly at close range as they always were at long.
Ravnos got Draba, more versatility in minion control (Reality, Sensory
Overload), and a card that made Far Fatuus more playable (Amria).
Setites got um...better vampires. And more stuff like stuff they
already had.
Giovanni got a lot of great toolbox options.

All four clans are in better shape then they were before Final Nights.

The sets since then have been more inconsistent. Ravnos got
Mayaparasatya, which is far stronger than anything else the other
three have gotten since Final Nights came out. But the sets have been
consistent in supporting each group seperately -- Sabbat, Indies, Cam,
then new stuff (BL and Anarchs), now we've gone back to the Sabbat.
It's time to go back to the Indies, and hopefully Gehenna will have
some good toys (though being a story-based expansion, I expect it to
be a bit more across-the-board in the support area).

If Gehenna doesn't give the indies a boost specifically, then whatever
comes next certainly should.

Fanboy

Messages.Author: Curevei

>> What I haven't noticed is a pattern where the putting
>> out of powerful sets has killed a CCG.
>
>Netrunner. Babylon 5. Galactic Empires. Highlander. Pokemon. The Star
>Wars CCG, in general. The Star Trek CCG, in general.

Are you sure about some of these? My sense is that Netrunner went away because
WotC stopped caring about anything that wasn't making boatloads of money.
Pokemon is still around, having taken a major hit because it isn't the in thing
anymore seemingly rather than the quality of any of its sets. First Star Wars
CCG ran out of images from the original trilogy. Star Trek recently rebooted
itself, was always an ass game from what I heard, yet is still alive because
anything Star Trek or Star Wars or, now, Lord of the Rings can apparently make
money.

B5 I know a lot more about. What technically killed it was Precedence losing
the license while Anal Shock (Anla'shok) was being designed and right before
the much delayed Collector's Set was going to finally come out. What hurt it
first was the delay putting out Psi Corps followed by the uselessness of PC.
Wheel of Fire, which was far and away more powerful than the previous two sets
- Psi Corps and Severed Dreams - sold better than the previous set, SD. SD was
probably the best designed but one of the weaker sets and likely suffered from
a PC hangover. Now, WoF likely also hurt the interest in the game as it did
the most to screw it up (with new mechanics that completely changed the nature
of the game), power escalation or no. The last set was probably the most
powerful, if not the most useful, but Anal Shock would have likely come out if
Pre. didn't waste its time on Rifts and put out expansions for their games that
were making money in a timely manner.

Actually, if I had to rate the number one reason a CCG will die outside of the
obvious two of being a junk game to begin with or being a quick money/fad game,
it would be taking too long between expansions. I'm not sure that's supported
in the big picture, but it drove me nuts with ones I played that we would lose
players because they'd get bored with the game.

>And, of course, the all-time best example -- Rage: Umbra.

I considered both Rages horrendous games that didn't deserve a player base, a
propos of just wanting to mention this.

>This doesn't happen with that *other* ccg for ONE REASON: there's too much
>money at stake for anyone to care that a particular set or sets can combine
>to make a "broken" season.

It helps that lots of people like playing Magic, even if lots don't. I've
heard plenty of Netrunner players bitch about constructed Netrunner. I hated
playing B5 at the end even though I was designing for it (ah, irony). Some,
small number of people I ran across enjoyed Rage, but it never seemed that
popular except maybe when it was brand new. Galactic Empires may have a
ridiculous number of expansions, but I hardly felt its presence, maybe because
it was before my time.

Messages.Author: Ben Swainbank
Messages.Body:
I too would like to some evolution in the game.

Some thoughts on how evolve the game without doing set rotation or
pure power escalation:

The currently clans and core disciplines are all well rounded and
developed at this point. I too would like Quietus and/or Assamites get
2-3 power cards, but that's the sole exception. And the vampire
selection for existing clans and discipline spreads is more than
sufficient.

I would like more discipline combinations to play with. Bloodlines
showed how 3-6 vamps with a set of common disciplines can make for a
solid deck core. Lets bust out the in-clan-3 formula and see small
clumps of vamps with NEC, VIC, CEL or THA, THN, MEL, OBF or POT, PRO,
SER. There's much freshness to be found with new combos of existing
disciplines- we just need the Vamps to form the crypt cores.

There are a number of underdeveloped card types, with inherent
disadvantages, that should come with above-the-curve effects.
Specifically, I'm thinking of Anarch-only cards, dual-discipline
cards, and Merged Vampire specials. All of these come with integrated
limitations. So, they provide a means to escalate the effects without
unbalancing new cards vs old.

Diversion is a good example of a 3-Way done well. It provides 3
different basic-level effects with the strength of advanced effects.
But, its Anarch-only. It's a nice example of power-escalation without
have an unbalancing effect, and can be the template for future 3-way
costing and balancing.

Dual-Discipline cards are really underused. Here again, the increased
discipline requirements should come with a power increase to offset
the cost. Basic duals should provide advanced effects and Advanced
duals can go over the top (especially for those discipline combos that
aren't in-clan for anyone).

Merged vampires are another, new, and under-developed mechanic.
Actually, building a crypt that has a reasonable chance of producing a
Merged vampire comes with a considerable cost. So, these merged
specials better be worth building a competitive deck around, or
there's not much point. A Merged Vampire should have some obvious
advantage over her non-merged brethren (other than
yet-another-conerncase-special) to make the crypt-contortions
worthwhile.

These are a few suggestions, some of which may already be the within
the intent of recent (and future?) sets. But I think this is the way
forward. 1) Provide new discipline combos. 2) Introduce new cards,
which, in some cases, provide more powerful effects than we've seen
(so we want to buy and build a deck around them!) but are balanced vs.
the older stuff with inherent limitations.

-Ben Swainbank

Messages.Author: Aramis
Messages.Body:
As someone who plays the Assamites extensively I'd tend to agree that
Assamites tend to need better actions. Assamites exist almost
entirely as a combat clan and right now the only actions they take are
the rush actions which lead them to combat. Sure, Clandestine
Contract was a great boon to Assamites, but it didn't really make the
combats any better except for allowing greater use of Khabar: Honor
and Provisions of the Silsila and the pool cost was quite prohibitive
for a clan with such poor pool gain and pool defense options.

I'd really like to see a follow-up on the Blood Clots-type of card. I
think pre-emptive weakening of targets via actions is exactly the kind
of theme I'd want for a clan of assassins. Of course these cards
would have to be much more powerful than Erosion or Blood Clots
otherwise they'd probably be passed over due to the difficulty of
increasing the action count of a standard Assamite deck. I think most
powerful effects could be balanced if the card was removable as an
action, or perhaps burned itself in the Assamite player's next untap
or some such.

I'd also submit that as a design goal the Assamites really should
focus on ousting their prey via combat instead of knocking all the
vampires down and bleeding for 1 alot. The contract concept was much
improved with Final Nights, but what is still lacking is a way for
Assamites to translate their combat power into ousting power. Fame
and Tension in the Ranks have both served as the baseline for any
combat-specific ousting method, but I think the Assamites should
receive a clan-specific card that adds to combat-induced pool damage
to reflect this clan's emphasis. I think this would best be
implemented via an action requiring an Assamite that puts the action
card in play and acts much in the same way as Tension in the Ranks for
the Assamite's controller, probably burnable as a (D) action like Army
of Rats.

Aramis

them as they see fit*

Messages.Author: Hollowboy
Messages.Body:
Curevei wrote:

It's not that I care whether the Assamites
> > are the best clan in the game for 6 months, but I do care that some currently
> > lesser clans get their moment in the sun, so to speak. And, really, over the

> > titles should be abbreviated in tournament winning decks as P/J are, and so

>

> The ways to accomplish that are by power escalation or by card set rotation
> (rotating out the old "good" cards).
>
> Which are you proposing (or is there something else you had in mind)?

I'm happy to chip in with a third (something else) way: give the weak
deck types multiuse cards, with some mild uses, plus one use which is
a hoser for the strategies that are too powerful.

Examples follow. Assumption for the examples are:

Anarchs and Assamites are the weakest strategy / clan
AND
Of the various powerful strategies, weenie vote and sneaky bleed need
targeting the most, as being quite tedious / frustrating for other
players.
AND
It was decided to alter this balance without escalating Anarchs and
Assamites to be the most powerful force in the game.

Please no-one respond to disagree with these assumptions. It doesn't
matter whether they are right or wrong - they are just there to
illustrate the concept. Anyway, assumption bit done. How could this
aim be achieved?

IMO, it would be possible by giving a selection of cards *only
playable by Assamites or Anarchs* which have several widely different
uses (in much the same way that Govern or Dreams have effects thet
differ in type, rather than just in power).

Have one use be generic, not too strong, and giving mild support to
what the Assamites / Anarch are already likely to be doing. Have one
use be strong in terms of effect per cost, BUT only usable against the
targeted powerful strategy.

Basically, have them be strategy hosers rather than clan hosers, and
cards which are playable in their own right, so it's possible /
sensible to include several of each in a regular deck.

That way, you would want to play the weak groups not because they will
dominate the game with their new cards, but specifically because the
new cards will let these formerly weak groups be the "scissors" to the
"paper" of the particular strategies that you are getting tired of.

Example cards:

Dreams of the Assamites
Type: Master (unique)
Pool Cost: 1
Clan Required: Assamite

Put a counter on this card each time you tap it; when the third
counter is added, burn this card.

Tap this card to give an Assamite you control one maneuver.

Tap when an Assamite announces a hunting action. If that action is
successful, the Assamite gains an additional blood.

Tap this card when a bleed for 2 or more is resolving at 2 or more
stealth. Reduce the bleed amount by 1, and inflict 2 points of damage
on the acting minion.

...2 OK abilities, + 1 which is quite powerful because you can hit any
stealth bleeder on the table with it... but which is no good if no-one
is playing stealth bleed.

Similarly:

Govern the Quietus
Type: Action
Blood Cost: 1
Discipline: Quietus

+1 stealth action
qui: choose up to 3 younger vampires. These vampires each move 1 blood
from themselves to their controllers blood pool.

QUI: burn a titled vampire whose capacity is less than 5.

...so one OK ability, can be used for pool gain, or aggressively with
Foul Blood or whatever, plus a rather harsh but limited-use hoser.

And anarchs could have a similar couple of cards...

Dreams of Anarchy
Type: Master (unique)
Pool Cost: 1

Requires a ready Anarch

Put a counter on this card each time you tap it; when the third
counter is added, burn this card.

Tap this card to allow a reacting Anarch to burn 1 blood to gain 2
votes.

Tap this card to move 2 blood from the blood bank to an Anarch in
torpor.

Tap this card when you are bled at more than 1 stealth to place a
grudge counter on the acting minion. Any Anarch may take a (D) action
to steal 2 blood or life from any minion with a grudge counter.

...again, its useful + useful + hoser.

And an action:

Govern the Anarchs
Type: Equipment
Pool cost: 1

Requires a ready Anarch

The anarch with this equipment may steal 1 blood from a younger
vampire as a +1 stealth action.

Burn this equipment and tap the Anarch bearing it to burn a titled
vampire whose capacity is below 5.

Yes, anyone can steal these ideas, WW can go nuts with them if it
wants to. No, I don't care too much about minuatae of card text (or
spelling, or whatever), it's the broad idea that matters.

Cheerio,
Craig

Messages.Author: Curevei
Messages.Body:
>Then perhaps what Clan Assamite [and other combat-centric clans] need
>is for combat to be amped into a more viable oust strategy. Rather
>than boost QUI or other specific disciplines, perhaps what needs to be
>addressed is the flaws of combat as a general strategy, and it's
>massive shortcomings when held up against S/B, votes, etc.

This would be fine if combat's balance flaws got worked on as well. I'm not
currently in favor of anything that encourages combat because combat is too
extreme and the table destabilization potential is high. Now, in the grand
scheme of things, more combat leads to more combat defense, which should
balance things out*. But, I'd be worried about a more chaotic environment when
significant but few changes are made in an area that doesn't lend itself to
balance in the first place rather than a better one.

* Though, there's a possible combat avoidance increase effect that can come
about as well.

>Burning a minion in combat is a hell of a lot harder than "Govern,
>Lost in crowds, Conditioning". Should the rewards not reflect this?

My view is that burning a minion should be nigh impossible and that it's its
own reward. Antiminion effects, whether noncombat or combat, everything else
being equal, reward playing lower cap vampires.

>Fair day's pay for a fair day's work and all that.

Except, I see little that's fair about combat. Or, more specifically,
individual combats. On average, things work out adequately, but individual
combats are far too extreme. The more rewards added to playing a combat
strategy, the more often these unfair events will occur.

And, there are other ways of helping combat besides rewarding it more heavily.
Reducing the ability to stealth actions through would see more combat, a
greater need to run combat defense in noncombat decks, which would in turn see
more combat as deck space is taken up with cards that don't evade combat.

Getting back to helping clans already good at combat, not every combat capable
clan or set of disciplines is weak. A *lot* of the imbalance in the game
arises from who has bounce and who doesn't. A decent disciplineless bounce
might reshape the landscape in desired ways. OTOH, how much do you want to
help the FoS or whoever at the same time?

I certainly think the merged mechanic has been a waste. There are a lot of

merged vampire, then the payoffs are so low as to not make it worth it unless
you would play the two vampires in your crypt anyway.

I think it's underpowered. I don't find the versatility great enough to offset

I really dislike the dual discipline cards in the game. Some are way too good
for the ease of play just ramping up the power level of clans (or, if you don't
like clans, vampires with easily found sets of disciplines) who don't need the
help. The Call, Madman's Quill, Read the Winds, Shroud of Absence - why do we
need these cards? Then, on the flip side, there are junky cards that do next
to nothing to elevate clans that could use help. Shadow Feint is kind of cool,
but the clans who play it easily could use something much better than kind of
cool. Even others annoy me; Nightmare Curse, yeah, I wanted another Sens. Dep.
in the game.

I think there's potential for good dual/multi disciplines, but I'd like to see
a lot better job done on execution: no more ones that just ramp up strong
clans, no more that suck, no more hosers, no more that make the game more
unpleasant to play. And, if those criteria aren't hard enough to satisfy, if
you do make a mistake, could you make the next Shroud of Absence common at
least?

>Merged vampires are another, new, and under-developed mechanic.
>Actually, building a crypt that has a reasonable chance of producing a
>Merged vampire comes with a considerable cost. So, these merged
>specials better be worth building a competitive deck around, or

*Competitive*

Merged vampire decks are combo decks and they get so little reward for their
combo. So with you.

I like them, and the Assasin's Path *is* thematically cute, but I do

combat-heavy (like where I live), it's already hard to play anything
BUT combat, or with quite a pile of combat defence (S:CE, chump
blockers, never using big caps unless they have fortitude). I think

potence option), that balance could be tipped a bit too far towards
combat, making it suicidal to play any decks / clans without
fortitude.

If whack-a-mole cards were to be developed, I would prefer to see them
either targeted towards truly obnoxious weenies (like Caitiff Princes
/ Pander Archbishops) or to have these cards go only to vampires which
can't prevent damage, so therefore only fight well in a lowish combat
environment. That way, environments that are already combat heavy
won't get crazy with nothing but bloodshed.

An example would be:

Brutal Demagogue
Type: Master
Clan: !Bruhaj or !Toreador
Text: Put this card on a ready titled Bruhaj Antitribune or Toreador
Antitribune you control. Only usable in combat when the younger
opposing vampire should go to torpor. This vampire may diablerize the
opposing vampire instead. If the opposing vampires capacity was below
5, this diablerising vampire gains 4 votes in the resulting blood
hunt. Not usable by a vampire going into torpor.

...in a low combat metagame, you could put slap this card onto Sela or
Amelia in a !Bru rush deck, or get it onto a !Tor eternal Vigilance
deck, for blazing pistolero carnage. But in a combat heavy metagame,
where Drawing out the beast and aggravated damage are more likely,
this card would be a lot harder to use, and therefore not tip the
balance towards even more combat.

Messages.Author: Joshua Duffin

> In fact I hate Life in the city, as it is an awfull boost to
> weenies/lowcaps and a hindrance to fatties (who cannot always afford
> to use one of the precious seven slots in your hand to gain a blood).

That's interesting. I haven't viewed it that way at all.

To me, weenies are much more able to afford the action to hunt to gain a
blood than fatties; as such they don't have as much need for Life in the
City, most of the time. Sure, they can use it, but they have to weigh
whether it's worth a card slot compared to being able to cardless-hunt
instead.

The "slot in hand" cost doesn't seem to me weighted against fatties.
Big-vampire decks, in my experience, are likely to cycle *fewer* cards
per turn than small-vampire decks; as such, the cost of having one of
them be a master card is often lower (since you weren't going to cycle
through all your cards anyway with minion actions) than for a weenie
deck. You could argue that the "master slot in deck" cost is still
pretty high for fattie decks, on the basis that with few vampires they
need each card to have maximum "effect per slot" value. But saving a
fatty from a mandatory hunt seems to me quite a bit stronger than saving
a weenie from a mandatory hunt.

> Another problem is that I still need to see an efficient way to
> destroy a bunch of embraces/progeny/thin blood seers through combat,
> which should thematically be easy but in fact isn't.

Yes, I do like your card ideas there. Cool concepts. :-)

I fail to see the difference. Not that I don't think that PTO is
unhealthy for the game, it is simply that I do not agree with your
reasoning.

The ability in and of itself to burn a vampire with a vote is very
much acceptable. The problem is that in PTO's (and IMHO Goratrix's and
maybe Akhenaten's) case the effect on the game balance and player
morale is very detrimental (especially due to the scale of the
effect). The reason I'm not so sure about Akhenaten is that it can be
countered by many types of offence/defence, whereas an IC or Goratrix,
adv. is far more sturdy.

I would reword Protect Thine Own's main text to be something like
this:

Political card, worth 1 vote. Called by any Justicar, Cardinal, or
Inner Circle member.
Cost: 2 Pool.
Choose a vampire with a capacity below 6. Succesful vote burns the
chosen vampire.
If this acting vampire is Regent or a member of the Inner Circle, this
action costs 2 pool less (but never less than 0 pool).

...or:

Political card, worth 1 vote. Called by any Justicar, or Inner Circle
member.
Cost: 1 Blood.
Choose a vampire with a capacity below 6. Succesful vote burns the
chosen vampire.
If this acting vampire is a member of the Inner Circle, you may choose
any vampire.
Only one Protect Thine Own can be played in a game.

So. ;) Note that the omission is not an omission... ;)

Bye,

Daneel

>

> blood than fatties; as such they don't have as much need for Life in the

> whether it's worth a card slot compared to being able to cardless-hunt
> instead.
>
> The "slot in hand" cost doesn't seem to me weighted against fatties.
> Big-vampire decks, in my experience, are likely to cycle *fewer* cards
> per turn than small-vampire decks; as such, the cost of having one of
> them be a master card is often lower (since you weren't going to cycle

IMHO the "slot cost" is higher for fatties because they often play
multiple disciplines, and thouch need wider card combinations. A
smallcap deck often plays 3-4 kinds of differnt cards massively,

>

They aren't well-rounded. But I think they are adequately developed.
I'm happy seeing focused disciplines. The clans (and the game) get
pretty bland once everyone can do everything.

>

So far, I agree. But I think that's mostly in the execution, rather
than the concept. Now that we have a better sense of the "cost" of

appropriately. Make then stronger and therefore worth the effort.
>

It's not. I'm a little Diversion-obsessed at the moment (hmm... look
at the fortitude on those Assamites... and the celerity on those
Ravnos... and the celerity and thaumaturgy on the !Ventrue!) Once you
get more then one discipline on a vamp and/or crypt its really quite

This is true of the 3-ways in general. Mole is also good. Smash and

requirement (even with in-clan disciplines) does its job here.

Agreed. Here is where there is room for improvement.

Right. Or, at least, make it free.

>

Yes.

Messages.Author: Joshua Duffin
Messages.Body:
"Emmanuel Martin" <e...@boursorama.com> wrote in message

news:10c2c156.04011...@posting.google.com...

[re life in the city]

> IMHO the "slot cost" is higher for fatties because they often play
> multiple disciplines, and thouch need wider card combinations. A
> smallcap deck often plays 3-4 kinds of differnt cards massively,
> whereas a fattie plays more different card from the combos he can pull
> out. So he needs more "drawing" new cards, especially while engaged in
> an action. Suppose you call a vote. You replace it with life in the
> city. Wouldn't you have prefered to draw voter cap instead ?

In that example, sure. I could also come up with examples where you'd
rather draw a Life in the City. (You play Wake during your predator's
turn and block an action, reducing your fatty to 0 blood. You draw
Voter Captivation during your untap phase. Wouldn't you rather have
drawn Life in the City, instead of being forced to hunt?)

I think I see what you're getting at, which seems to be the idea that
weenies can "afford" to use cards that have a relatively small effect
individually, because their many minion actions let them accumulate
effectiveness over many actions instead of just a few. I would still
say that a weenie deck benefits a lot less from saving a single weenie
from having to hunt than a fatty deck benefits from keeping its fatty
from having to hunt. But I think you're saying that the weenie deck
doesn't *need* to get as much benefit, because it's already got the
"weenie advantage" overall.

Which is probably true as far as it goes, but I'm not sure it's a good
argument to show that Life in the City actually *helps* weenie decks
more than fatty decks. Since the weenie deck doesn't benefit all that
much from it, even if it can get *some* use out of the card because each
card doesn't *have* to do that much in its deck, I'm not yet convinced
that LitC is truly a card that helps weenies more than fatties. (I've
played it in relatively-fat decks and liked having it there myself.)

Josh

Yep, I can see why you made it. But, I proposed an alternative version

Yes, I can see that you want to hose annoying weenie decks where you

I wouldn't want to see any new cards created that helped to hose most

them being easily burned, I would have to play fatties. And if I play
fatties, I can't afford to lose one, so I must play with fortitude.
That's pretty limiting.
