Messages.Body:
> This would be fine if combat's balance flaws got worked on as well. I'm not
> currently in favor of anything that encourages combat because combat is too
> extreme and the table destabilization potential is high.

"Too extreme"? Please define.

> Now, in the grand scheme of things, more combat leads to more combat defense, which should balance things out*. But, I'd be worried about a more chaotic environment when significant but few changes are made in an area that doesn't lend itself to balance in the first place rather than a better one.

"Does not lend itself to balance"? Please explain.

> My view is that burning a minion should be nigh impossible and that it's its
> own reward. Antiminion effects, whether noncombat or combat, everything else
> being equal, reward playing lower cap vampires.

There is little to no reward in burning a minion. Provision of the
Silsila, Draught of the Soul and Tension in the Ranks are the only
cards [that i can think of off the top of my head] that generate any
kind of direct profit from the incredibly difficult task of actually
ashing a minion through combat. Bragging rights is about the best most
decks get out of it, and they don't pay the bills.

> Except, I see little that's fair about combat. Or, more specifically,
> individual combats. On average, things work out adequately, but individual
> combats are far too extreme. The more rewards added to playing a combat
> strategy, the more often these unfair events will occur.

Again, please explain what is "unfair" about combat?

> And, there are other ways of helping combat besides rewarding it more heavily.
> Reducing the ability to stealth actions through would see more combat, a
> greater need to run combat defense in noncombat decks, which would in turn see
> more combat as deck space is taken up with cards that don't evade combat.

"Reducing stealth" would require nerfing or banning the current
stealth cards in play - not really a viable option. Increasing the
abilities of intercept is a more realistic option, but so long as
"block fails, block with someone else" cards like Elder intervention
and Call of the hungry Dead exist, even this isn't a very sure bet.

> Getting back to helping clans already good at combat, not every combat capable
> clan or set of disciplines is weak. A *lot* of the imbalance in the game
> arises from who has bounce and who doesn't. A decent disciplineless bounce
> might reshape the landscape in desired ways. OTOH, how much do you want to
> help the FoS or whoever at the same time?

FOS have their own unique problems which are somewhat off thread.

I'm talking about making combat a more competitive and viable ousting
strategy than it is now [easily the weakest fo the bleed/vote/combat
pantheon]. At the moment, if you actually win a tourney with a combat
deck, you're generally regarded as having turned water into wine.

noodleboy

Messages.Author: Jeff Kuta
Messages.Body:
nood...@iprimus.net.au (noodleboy) wrote in message news:<e72ec49.04011...@posting.google.com>...

> > Except, I see little that's fair about combat. Or, more specifically,
> > individual combats. On average, things work out adequately, but individual
> > combats are far too extreme. The more rewards added to playing a combat
> > strategy, the more often these unfair events will occur.
>
> Again, please explain what is "unfair" about combat?

The point of combat is to destroy another person's game by eliminating
their minions. You either deal pool damage to them as a result of them
failing in combat, or bleed them when they're defenseless after all
their minions are either burnt or in torpor.

Whether this is "fair" or not is debateable--it's combat right? So
everyone has the same playing field to start--but when tiny minions
can wreck huge minions it can cause "unfair" swings in the game, e.g.
Koko catches Arika at the wrong time and Amaranth's her. Sure Koko's
controller had to get lucky, but a 2-cap burning an 11-cap should be
nearly impossible if the game were realistic. Yeah, you can say that
Arika should have been playing more Fortitude, but just because the
cards make it possible doesn't mean it should be possible.

Personally, I like combat a lot and don't have much of a problem with
small vampires burning large vampires (especially Tariq). But when
11-pool worth of someone's resources goes up in a single event, it can
be perceived as "unfair" simply because that's 1/3 of a person's game
gone in a very short time. These huge swings in table balance due to a
single action--ANY ACTION--are what's most problematic.

Messages.Author: Curevei
Messages.Body:
>> This would be fine if combat's balance flaws got worked on as well. I'm
>not
>> currently in favor of anything that encourages combat because combat is too
>> extreme and the table destabilization potential is high.
>
>"Too extreme"? Please define.

Some common results of a combat between two vampires:
One or both play combat ends and nothing happens.
One or both maneuver and wave or dodge and nothing happens.
One or both are "real" combat decks and one or both vampires end up torpored or
(less likely) burnt.

BTW, while exchanging hands for 1 may be a common result, it can't be that
common as I've run into problems cycling Martyr's Resiliences in games.

I don't know what the average blood loss is per vampire per combat. Let's say
the mean is 2 as a basis for trying to clarify the point. While the mean may
be 2, the mode results are far more often 0, 1, 3+. Combat is extreme in that
it rarely matches the average.

Nothing happens combat is the death of some combat decks. Torp/burn results
can randomly end someone's, anyone's game. Again, as it stands, on average for
a game, combat works out much better, but each individual combat has the
potential to be fraught with peril.

Then, because combat comes in much more diverse forms, it's far harder to
metagame against than bleed or vote, leading to a greater luck/match up factor.

It wouldn't have to be at all about having Celerity or Potence do
"everything", though. That's an *easy* way to develop them in
directions other than the "99.44% combat cards" direction they've mostly
been in, but they *could*... in theory... get unique new effects that
made them interesting in ways other than "beating people up, a lot,
really fast". Action cards that do weird wacky stuff, for example
(things as unduplicated as Masochism or Army of Rats or Contagion). Or
action modifiers more in the vein of Perfect Clarity and less in the
vein of Alacrity. Or even combat cards that don't just produce +damage
or +strikes or dodges or maneuvers.

There's already been some clear effort in this direction, with things
like Rooftop Shadow (though it is a "somewhat" generic effect), Brick
Laying, and so on. More of that would, IMO, be cool. Especially for
the disciplines that are currently very "narrow" in terms of what kinds
of effects are available to them.

innate ability of Goratrix, Advanced. Also, IMHO some of the votes are
less particular.

Also note that a lot of the common threats can be made direct any
methuselah with certain decks. Malkavians can bleed any methuselah
with Kindred Spirits, Assamites can rush anyone with Contracts or (D)
rushes, etc. In fact, on a tournament I'm usually using a decks that
can harm cross-table to maintain the game balance. There were issues
where I eliminated someone from across the table (to win the game
later, of course).

My concern is that PTO is too cheap. Many times have my grand-predator
passed the harmful votes while my crippled predator was still in the
game (effectively making blocking them impossible). In this respect I
agree with your reasoning, even if I'm not sure repeatable (D) actions
are morally less puzzling. If Goratrix, Advanced sits cross-table and
wants to burn my Tremere Antitribu every round, I'm not sure I'll feel
too comfortable. Or if my ally plays DI from cross-table to burn my
bounce card.

My general problem is that these are two separate issues - ganging up
and too powerful effect. You seem to be concerned by the first issue,
while I'm more concerned about the latter. My take is that ganging up
cannot be ruled out, its observation should be vigilantly done by the
judges to prevent unsportsmanship. However, the likes of PTO and
Goratrix, Advanced have the possibility of being the only currently
possible action that can cripple a particular deck in a defenceless
moment (after a conceptually necessary round of overexpansion, etc).

I'll leave it at that, as my last sentence fairly well explains why I
dislike PTO.

Regards,

Daneel

Reaction
Cost = 1
<cel>: Play when a directed action is announced that targets this minion. The

(if any) back into his or her hand (and discards down to his or her hand size),

interchangeable. If you don't care about the differences in abilities, then
it's strictly better to run one of each than two of one, as you said.

much of a benefit. Then, merged, I'm not impressed by the gains over the basic

either merged ability. The former being even more effort for a deck already
going to the effort of merging a vampire; the latter being ho hum with a
vampire with a strong bleed discipline.

the new concept is something everyone else will do as well because it's the
only effective thing you can do with the cards at hand.

Typhonic Beast as Ser/Pre would still suck. It doesn't fulfill a useful role.
If it were free, then at least it would be light combat defense. But, rush

as Dem/Pre? Okay, I can see the point of its existence now. A fairly strong

multidiscipline cards in other inclan combinations wouldn't.

>probably be more powerful than the older version (more Superior

Still not seeing enough payoff in trying to merge.

isn't critical? I'm guessing you mean build around one of them when they are
largely interchangeable, emphasizing the idea that you can reduce crypt
duplication. But, I'd go back to how little you get for *trying* to merge
vampires. If the intent is only that merging is a random event that happens
when you get the right crypt draw, then the individual vampires should be
costed well and not costed as if they were always going to be merged. If the
intent is to see merged vampire decks, then the payoff needs to be greater to
justify the limitations put on deck construction and other costs associated
with merging.

>PS Why doesn't Tusk have a merged ability?!? Who was responsible for
>that???

One assumes the process was something like:
"What would be really funny is making an advanced group 1 vampire like Tusk."
"That would be funny. He couldn't be played with our new base set Nos we just
released."
"Even funnier - we make him worse than the original and give no good reason to
play with both."
"Brilliant!"

Underdeveloped? Ignoring bloodlines, I'd still say the Sabbat clans, with the
possible exceptions of the Lasombra and Tzimisce. The antitribu are in every
case weaker than the originals, though it varies how much so. Also, they tend
to do the same things the originals do, not unsurprising given the discipline
combination similarities. One of the good things about BH is that makes the
antitribu a bit more distinct. Still, the number of clan specific cards
heavily favors the Cammies. The Cam title cards are better. Makes some sense
that the Cammies come out better per clan as there are fewer Cam clans. Then,
there are the Pander who do little but provide weenie support.

Underpowered? Similar story but add in the Assamites. Assuming things change
for the !Brujah and !Nos post-BH, which is a bit of an assumption, !Gangrel and
Assamites need the most help.

If you look at disciplines, I'd diversify Celerity and Potence, give some
decent stuff to Thaumaturgy, Serpentis, and Quietus.

Bloodlines? They could all use something. Ahrimanes could use a Gangrel or
!Gangrel with ANI/PRE or could use another Bear Paw. Spiritus having some more
variety wouldn't hurt either. Baali could use a change in the infernal rule
that read "infernal means nothing". BB could use a good strategy that has no
synergy with Unwholesome Bond. DoC could use another vampire so that Choir
sucked less. Gargoyles? Maybe a blood gain card along the lines of Taste or
Kamut. HoS could use a little helper dude. Kiasyd could use a card that makes
them less Lasombralike. Nagaraja could use something that ties them together.
Samedi could use intercept and an across the board reduction in capacity.
Salubri could use an ally. !Salubri could use help, a lot of help. True
Brujah could use intercept and/or bounce, but, then, couldn't every clan?

The effect of Banishment is actually very similar to that of PTO.

In my experience, a cross-table PTO is used when you are about
to oust your prey and you want to weaken your grandprey; or
when there is a vampire threatening the whole table or yourself
(such as a Fatima [in a multirush deck], Lucita [in a turbo
deck], etc.); or when your grandpredator is about to oust your
predator and is a real threat to you; or in other cases I cannot
remember now.

What's the difference between playing a PTO and a Banishment
when you are about to deal a final blow?.

PTO only affects non-Camarilla vampires and can only be
effectively called by the 7 Inner Circle members. While
Banishment can be called by any older vampire and can
affect any younger vampire (regardless of sect allegiance
and title).

In the mid or end game, vampires are not usually at full
capacity, so Banishment's effect can be as much destructive
as PTO's, since the result is the same: you lose a vampire.
(note that when dealing a final blow, losing a vampire for
1 or 2 turns is the same as losing a vampire forever,
because you cannot use that vampire anyway, and you might
not have enough pool to influence him back into play later).

Messages.Author: Daneel
Messages.Body:
> >What justification do you have that Political Actions, as opposed to other
> >actions which don't ask permission of the table, be denied the ability to burn
> >vampires?
>
> Cross table targetting and the inability of the victim to even attempt
> to block.

Nice. I'm just back from a relatively prominent tournament (~55
people), and I just have first-hand experience of how cross-table
targetting really works.

In a game my predator had vote control (by having certain vote
cancellation tools and some votes) in a fashion that no political deck
could pass any votes without his approval or consent.

Therefor all political actions done by my predator's predator and his
predator (my hypothetical allies) and my prey (luckily everyone had at
least a small voting angle in their deck) ended up putting (or trying
to put) at least some of the pool loss and other detrimental effects
on me. Distinguished as I felt for such an honor I nevertheless begun
wondering whether the problem is not with the nature of politics.

Because even though PTO could have burned my 7-cap vampire in a single
action, over the course of several turns the small leftovers from KRCs
and CAs amounted to a fair loss (which, among other circumstances,
eventually ended up in my oust).

I begun to develop a certain dislike towards politics in general.
Because given my preference for non-political decks I usually end up
getting shafted by these cross-table votes, even if I pack lots of
intercept (as I did today).

So all in all politics in general is unfair, because voting decks have
a tendency to weaken their prey *and* the prey of the other most
prominent voting power - meaning, they usually target cross table just
to get their thing done. PTO does not really stand out from among the
other political cards regarding this.

PTO does stand out in power and effect though.

So all in all I'm on the opposite side of the same side regarding
PTO... ;)

Bye,

Daneel
